### V-280987 · RHEL-10-200644 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must authenticate the remote logging server for off-loading audit logs via "rsyslog".

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280987r1195371_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000342-GPOS-00133 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-001851 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must authenticate the remote logging server for off-loading audit logs via "rsyslog".

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/rsyslog.d/99-forwarding.conf | streamdriver.authmode | "x509/name" |
| Config | /etc/rsyslog.d/99-forwarding.conf | streamdriver.permittedpeer | "rsyslog.server.example.com" |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, admin_space_left(_action), disk_full_action, disk_error_action, max_log_file(_action), action_mail_acct). Off-loading uses rsyslog (omfwd with TLS via gtls/ossl stream drivers) or the audisp-remote / audit 'remote' plugin. Put /var/log/audit on its own partition so it can't starve the root file system. Restart with 'service auditd restart', because systemctl is blocked for auditd.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 authenticates the remote logging server for off-loading audit logs with the following command:

$ sudo grep -r -E 'streamdriver.authmode|streamdriver.permittedpeer|tls.authmode|tls.permittedpeer' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/
/etc/rsyslog.d/99-forwarding.conf:        streamdriver.authmode="x509/name"

If the variable name "streamdriver.authmode" is present in an omfwd statement block, this is not a finding. However, if the "streamdriver.authmode" variable is in a module block, this is a finding.

If the value of the "$ActionSendStreamDriverAuthMode" or "streamdriver.authmode" or "tls.authmode" option is not set to "x509/name", or the line is commented out, ask the system administrator to indicate how the audit logs are off-loaded to a different system or media.

Additionally, if the permittedpeer is not specified in either of the following formats, this is a finding:
streamdriver.permittedpeer="rsyslog.server.example.com"
tls.permittedpeer="rsyslog.server.example.com"

If there is no evidence that the transfer of the audit logs being off-loaded to another system or media is encrypted, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to authenticate the remote logging server for off-loading audit logs by setting the following options in "/etc/rsyslog.d/99-forwarding.conf":

streamdriver.authmode="x509/name"

Specify the logserver to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks in the following format:
streamdriver.permittedpeer="rsyslog.server.example.com"
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Information stored in one location is vulnerable to accidental or incidental deletion or alteration.

Off-loading is a common process in information systems with limited audit storage capacity.

RHEL 10 installation media provides "rsyslogd", a system utility providing support for message logging. Support for both internet and Unix domain sockets enables this utility to support both local and remote logging. Coupling this utility with "gnutls" (a secure communications library implementing the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL), Transport Layer Security (TLS), and Datagram TLS (DTLS) protocols) creates a method to securely encrypt and off-load auditing.

The "rsyslog" supported authentication modes include:
- anon - Anonymous authentication.
- x509/fingerprint - Certificate fingerprint authentication.
- x509/certvalid - Certificate validation only.
- x509/name - Certificate validation and subject name authentication.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000342-GPOS-00133, SRG-OS-000479-GPOS-00224

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001851**: Transfer audit logs per organization-defined frequency to a different system, system component, or media than the system or system component conducting the logging.  
  Rev 5: AU-4 (1) · Rev 4: AU-4 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 encrypts audit records offloaded onto a different system via rsyslog using the modern "omfwd" action.

Search for active TLS-enabling configurations within "omfwd" action blocks with the following command:

$ sudo grep -rE 'tls="on"|StreamDriver.Mode\s*=\s*"1"' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/

If an active TCP-based "omfwd" forwarding rule exists on the system but the command above returns no active configuration lines, or if all results are commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to encrypt off-loaded audit records via rsyslog by enabling TLS within the "omfwd" action rule.

action(
  type="omfwd"
  target="logserver.example.com"
  protocol="tcp"
  port="6514"
  tls="on"
)

After applying the configuration, restart the rsyslog service:
$ sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
```

### V-280990 · RHEL-10-200647 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must monitor all remote access methods.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280990r1268219_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000032-GPOS-00013 |
| Topic | Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-000067 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-17 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-17 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-17 (1) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must monitor all remote access methods.

**Why it matters:** Administrators can control computers from far away, as if they were sitting at the keyboard. This rule makes sure those remote connections are encrypted, require a proper sign-in every time, and can't be used to copy files around carelessly. It's like requiring a video-verified, recorded call before anyone can give orders over the phone.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, X11 forwarding ('X11Forwarding no' in sshd), VNC servers and cockpit are the main remote-access paths to restrict.

**Operational impact:** Disabling drive and clipboard redirection affects admin convenience. WinRM restrictions can break management tools that use Basic auth over HTTP (some older configuration-management and monitoring products), so move those to Kerberos or HTTPS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 monitors all remote access methods with the following command:

$ sudo grep -rE '(auth.\*|authpriv.\*|daemon.\*)' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/
/etc/rsyslog.conf:authpriv.*                                              /var/log/secure

If "auth.*", "authpriv.*", or "daemon.*" are not configured to be logged, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to monitor all remote access methods.

Add or update the following lines to the "/etc/rsyslog.conf" file or a file in "/etc/rsyslog.d":

auth.*;authpriv.*;daemon.* /var/log/secure

Restart the "rsyslog" service with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart rsyslog.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Logging remote access methods can be used to trace the decrease in the risks associated with remote user access management. It can also be used to spot cyberattacks and ensure ongoing compliance with organizational policies surrounding the use of remote access methods.

**Threat & control context:** Remote-management protocols give interactive or programmatic control of a host and are a favored vector for both ransomware operators and insiders. Requirements include encrypted transport, no Basic/Digest authentication or unencrypted WinRM traffic, always prompting for credentials, no saved RDP passwords, no drive redirection, and session time limits. These implement AC-17 (remote access), AC-17(2) (confidentiality and integrity via encryption), SC-8 and AC-12 (session termination).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000067**: Employ automated mechanisms to monitor remote access methods.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (1) · Rev 4: AC-17 (1) · Rev 3: AC-17 (1)

### V-280991 · RHEL-10-200648 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must use cron logging.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280991r1273567_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000040-GPOS-00018 |
| Topic | System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000133 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 d |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must use cron logging.

**Why it matters:** Computers run many background programs ("services") all the time. This rule makes sure the important security ones are always running and the unneeded or risky ones are switched off, like keeping the alarm system armed while unplugging the appliances you don't use.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Before masking a service, confirm nothing depends on it ('systemctl list-dependencies --reverse <unit>').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 rsyslog is configured to log cron events with the following command:

Note: If another logging package is used, substitute the utility configuration file for "/etc/rsyslog.conf" or "/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf" files.

$ grep -s "cron.\*" /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
/etc/rsyslog.d/99-cron-stig.conf:cron.* action(type="omfile" file="/var/log/cron")

If the command does not return a line demonstrating logging to /var/log/cron, perform a functional cron test.

Inject a message into the cron logging facility with the following command:

$ logger -p cron.info "STIG-TEST-CRON-LOGGING"

Check if it successfully wrote to the dedicated log file with the following command:

$ sudo grep "STIG-TEST-CRON-LOGGING" /var/log/cron
Jul 16 11:33:00 RHEL10Sim pdosadmin[33692]: STIG-TEST-CRON-LOGGING

If "rsyslog" is not logging messages for the cron facility or all facilities, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 rsyslog to log all cron messages by adding or updating the following line to "/etc/rsyslog.conf" or a configuration file in the /etc/rsyslog.d/ directory:

cron.* /var/log/cron

The rsyslog daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart rsyslog.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Cron logging can be used to trace the successful or unsuccessful execution of cron jobs. It can also be used to spot intrusions into the use of the cron facility by unauthorized and malicious users.

**Threat & control context:** Security functions such as auditd, firewalld, sshd's hardened configuration, fapolicyd and USBGuard only protect the system while their services are running. Conversely, every listening or socket-activated service is reachable attack surface. CM-7 (least functionality) and AU/SI controls require the security services to be enabled and the non-essential ones disabled or masked so they can't be started indirectly.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000133**: Ensure that audit records containing information that establishes the source of the event.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 d · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3

### V-280992 · RHEL-10-200650 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must have the packages required for encrypting off-loaded audit logs installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280992r1268232_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the packages required for encrypting off-loaded audit logs installed.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | rsyslog-gnutls | Installed |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, admin_space_left(_action), disk_full_action, disk_error_action, max_log_file(_action), action_mail_acct). Off-loading uses rsyslog (omfwd with TLS via gtls/ossl stream drivers) or the audisp-remote / audit 'remote' plugin. Put /var/log/audit on its own partition so it can't starve the root file system. Restart with 'service auditd restart', because systemctl is blocked for auditd.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 has the "rsyslog-gnutls" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list --installed rsyslog-gnutls
Installed Packages
rsyslog-gnutls.x86_64                                     8.2412.0-1.el10                                     @AppStream

If the "rsyslog-gnutls" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have the "rsyslog-gnutls" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install rsyslog-gnutls
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "rsyslog-gnutls" package provides Transport Layer Security (TLS) support for the rsyslog daemon, which enables secure remote logging.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000803**: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for such authentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-7 · Rev 4: IA-7 · Rev 3: IA-7

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "audit" package installed.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | audit | Installed |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. **Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
$ sudo dnf list --installed audit
```


#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without establishing what type of events occurred, along with the source, location, and outcome, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events leading up to an outage or attack.

Audit record content that may be necessary to satisfy this requirement includes, for example, time stamps, source and destination addresses, user/process identifiers, event descriptions, success/fail indications, filenames involved, and access control or flow control rules invoked.

Associating event types with detected events in audit logs provides a means of investigating an attack, recognizing resource utilization or capacity thresholds, or identifying an improperly configured RHEL 10 system.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000038-GPOS-00016, SRG-OS-000039-GPOS-00017, SRG-OS-000040-GPOS-00018, SRG-OS-000041-GPOS-00019, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00021, SRG-OS-000051-GPOS-00024, SRG-OS-000054-GPOS-00025, SRG-OS-000122-GPOS-00063, SRG-OS-000254-GPOS-00095, SRG-OS-000255-GPOS-00096, SRG-OS-000337-GPOS-00129, SRG-OS-000348-GPOS-00136, SRG-OS-000349-GPOS-00137, SRG-OS-000350-GPOS-00138, SRG-OS-000351-GPOS-00139, SRG-OS-000352-GPOS-00140, SRG-OS-000353-GPOS-00141, SRG-OS-000354-GPOS-00142, SRG-OS-000358-GPOS-00145, SRG-OS-000365-GPOS-00152, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000475-GPOS-00220

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

### V-280995 · RHEL-10-200662 · CAT III: RHEL 10 must have the "audispd-plugins" package installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280995r1195383_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000342-GPOS-00133 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling |
| CCI | CCI-001851 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "audispd-plugins" package installed.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | audispd-plugins | Installed |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, admin_space_left(_action), disk_full_action, disk_error_action, max_log_file(_action), action_mail_acct). Off-loading uses rsyslog (omfwd with TLS via gtls/ossl stream drivers) or the audisp-remote / audit 'remote' plugin. Put /var/log/audit on its own partition so it can't starve the root file system. Restart with 'service auditd restart', because systemctl is blocked for auditd.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 has the "audispd-plugins" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list --installed audispd-plugins
Installed Packages
audispd-plugins.x86_64                           4.0.3-1.el10                            @rhel-10-for-x86_64-baseos-rpms

If the "audispd-plugins" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have the "audispd-plugins" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install audispd-plugins
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "audispd-plugins" package provides plugins for the real-time interface to the audit subsystem, "audispd". These plugins can do such things as relay events to remote machines or analyze events for suspicious behavior.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001851**: Transfer audit logs per organization-defined frequency to a different system, system component, or media than the system or system component conducting the logging.  
  Rev 5: AU-4 (1) · Rev 4: AU-4 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-280996 · RHEL-10-200680 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must have the "libreswan" package installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280996r1268232_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software |
| CCI | CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "libreswan" package installed.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | libreswan | Installed |

**How it works:** On RHEL, remove packages with 'dnf remove <pkg>' and verify with 'rpm -q <pkg>' (expect 'package <pkg> is not installed'). Watch for dependency cascades in the dnf transaction summary before confirming.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If there is no operational need for Libreswan to be installed, this rule is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 has the "libreswan" service package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list --installed libreswan
Installed Packages
libreswan.x86_64                                         5.2-1.el10_0                                         @AppStream

If the "libreswan" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have the "libreswan" service package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install libreswan
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Providing the ability for remote users or systems to initiate a secure virtual private network connection protects information when it is transmitted over a wide area network.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000803**: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for such authentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-7 · Rev 4: IA-7 · Rev 3: IA-7

### V-280997 · RHEL-10-200690 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must notify designated personnel if baseline configurations are changed in an unauthorized manner.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280997r1195387_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000046-GPOS-00022 |
| Topic | Software & File Integrity Verification |
| CCI | CCI-000139 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-5 a |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must notify designated personnel if baseline configurations are changed in an unauthorized manner.

**Why it matters:** This makes the computer check a digital "seal" on software before installing it, and keep a fingerprint of important files so it can notice if anyone changes them. It's like checking that a medicine bottle's safety seal is intact, and noticing straight away if someone has tampered with it.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | postfix | Installed |

**How it works:** On RHEL, repositories must have 'gpgcheck=1' (/etc/dnf/dnf.conf and /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo) and 'localpkg_gpgcheck=1', with Red Hat GPG keys imported ('rpm -q gpg-pubkey'). AIDE is configured in /etc/aide.conf (rules should include acl, xattrs and sha512). Initialize with 'aide --init' and move the new database into place. Schedule 'aide --check' daily (cron or systemd timer) with notification to the SA/ISSO.

**Operational impact:** AIDE reports every legitimate change too, so re-baseline after approved patching and keep the database read-only or off-host. Internal repositories must sign their packages, or clients will refuse them.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to allow sending email notifications.

Note: The "postfix" package provides the "mail" command that is used to send email messages.

Verify that the "postfix" package is installed on the system:

$ sudo dnf list --installed postfix
Installed Packages
postfix.x86_64                                         2:3.8.5-8.el10                                         @AppStream

If the "postfix" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to notify designated personnel if baseline configurations are changed in an unauthorized manner.

Install the postfix package with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install postfix
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "postfix" package provides the mail command required to allow sending email notifications of unauthorized configuration changes to designated personnel.

**Threat & control context:** Signature verification ensures only vendor-authentic software is installed (CM-14 signed components, SI-7 software and information integrity). File-integrity monitoring such as AIDE detects unauthorized modification of binaries and configuration after the fact (SI-7(1), CM-3(5)), catching rootkits, backdoored binaries and configuration drift. The value of FIM depends on protecting the baseline database off-host and acting on alerts.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary; T1014 Rootkit

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000139**: Alert organization-defined personnel or roles within an organization-defined time period in the event of an audit logging process failure.  
  Rev 5: AU-5 a · Rev 4: AU-5 a · Rev 3: AU-5 a

### V-280998 · RHEL-10-200691 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must have mail aliases to notify the information system security officer (ISSO) and system administrator (SA) (at a minimum) of an audit processing failure.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280998r1208794_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000046-GPOS-00022 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000139 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-5 a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have mail aliases to notify the information system security officer (ISSO) and system administrator (SA) (at a minimum) of an audit processing failure.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, admin_space_left(_action), disk_full_action, disk_error_action, max_log_file(_action), action_mail_acct). Off-loading uses rsyslog (omfwd with TLS via gtls/ossl stream drivers) or the audisp-remote / audit 'remote' plugin. Put /var/log/audit on its own partition so it can't starve the root file system. Restart with 'service auditd restart', because systemctl is blocked for auditd.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to notify the appropriate interactive users of an audit processing failure.

Find the alias maps that are being used with the following command:

$ postconf alias_maps
alias_maps = lmdb:/etc/aliases

Query the Postfix alias maps for an alias for the root user with the following command:

$ postmap -q root lmdb:/etc/aliases
ISSO

If an alias is not set, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have mail aliases notify the ISSO and SA (at a minimum) of an audit processing failure.

Edit the aliases map file (by default /etc/aliases) used by Postfix and configure a root alias (using the user ISSO as an example):

root:    ISSO

Update the aliases database with the following command:

$ sudo newaliases
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** It is critical for the appropriate personnel to be aware if a system is at risk of failing to process audit logs as required. Without this notification, the security personnel may be unaware of an impending failure of the audit capability, and system operation may be adversely affected.

Audit processing failures include software/hardware errors, failures in the audit capturing mechanisms, and audit storage capacity being reached or exceeded.

This requirement applies to each audit data storage repository (i.e., distinct information system component where audit records are stored), the centralized audit storage capacity of organizations (i.e., all audit data storage repositories combined), or both.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000139**: Alert organization-defined personnel or roles within an organization-defined time period in the event of an audit logging process failure.  
  Rev 5: AU-5 a · Rev 4: AU-5 a · Rev 3: AU-5 a

### V-280999 · RHEL-10-200692 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured to prevent unrestricted mail relaying.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-280999r1165352_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to prevent unrestricted mail relaying.

**Why it matters:** Computers run many background programs ("services") all the time. This rule makes sure the important security ones are always running and the unneeded or risky ones are switched off, like keeping the alarm system armed while unplugging the appliances you don't use.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Before masking a service, confirm nothing depends on it ('systemctl list-dependencies --reverse <unit>').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If postfix is not installed, this is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 is configured to prevent unrestricted mail relaying with the following command:

$ postconf -n smtpd_client_restrictions
smtpd_client_restrictions = permit_mynetworks,reject

If the "smtpd_client_restrictions" parameter contains any entries other than "permit_mynetworks" and "reject", and the additional entries have not been documented with the information system security officer, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that the postfix configuration file restricts client connections to the local network with the following command:

$ sudo postconf -e 'smtpd_client_restrictions = permit_mynetworks,reject'
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If unrestricted mail relaying is permitted, unauthorized senders could use this host as a mail relay to send spam or for other unauthorized activity.

**Threat & control context:** Security functions such as auditd, firewalld, sshd's hardened configuration, fapolicyd and USBGuard only protect the system while their services are running. Conversely, every listening or socket-activated service is reachable attack surface. CM-7 (least functionality) and AU/SI controls require the security services to be enabled and the non-essential ones disabled or masked so they can't be started indirectly.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have a Secure Shell (SSH) server installed for all networked systems.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | openssh-server | Installed |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 has the "openssh-server" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list --installed openssh-server
Installed Packages
openssh-server.x86_64                                      9.9p1-7.el10_0                                      @anaconda

If the "openssh-server" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have the "openssh-server" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install openssh-server
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without protection of the transmitted information, confidentiality and integrity may be compromised because unprotected communications can be intercepted and read or altered.

This requirement applies to internal and external networks and all types of information system components from which information can be transmitted (e.g., servers, mobile devices, notebook computers, printers, copiers, scanners, and facsimile machines). Communication paths outside the physical protection of a controlled boundary are exposed to the possibility of interception and modification.

Protecting the confidentiality and integrity of organizational information can be accomplished by physical means (e.g., employing physical distribution systems) or by logical means (e.g., employing cryptographic techniques). If physical means of protection are employed, logical means (cryptography) do not have to be employed, and vice versa.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000423-GPOS-00187, SRG-OS-000424-GPOS-00188, SRG-OS-000425-GPOS-00189, SRG-OS-000426-GPOS-00190

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002418**: Protect the confidentiality and/or integrity of transmitted information.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 · Rev 4: SC-8 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002421**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of information and/or detect changes to information during transmission.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 (1) · Rev 4: SC-8 (1) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002420**: Maintain the confidentiality and/or integrity of information during preparation for transmission.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 (2) · Rev 4: SC-8 (2) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002422**: Maintain the confidentiality and/or integrity of information during reception.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 (2) · Rev 4: SC-8 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281005 · RHEL-10-200730 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must have the "pkcs11-provider" package installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281005r1273568_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000105-GPOS-00052 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000765, CCI-004046, CCI-001954 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-2 (1), IA-2 (6) (a), IA-2 (12) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 (1), IA-2 (12) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-2 (1) |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "pkcs11-provider" package installed.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | pkcs11-provider | Installed |

**How it works:** On RHEL, smart card login is handled by SSSD with 'pam_cert_auth = True', the certificate trust store configured in sssd.conf / /etc/sssd/pki/sssd_auth_ca_db.pem, and certificate mapping rules (matchrule/maprule). Revocation checking is configured with 'certificate_verification' (OCSP). authselect features such as 'with-smartcard' wire SSSD into PAM.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If the system administrator demonstrates the use of an approved alternate multifactor authentication method, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 has the "pkcs11-provider" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list --installed pkcs11-provider
Installed Packages
pkcs11-provider.x86_64                           1.0-3.el10_0                            @rhel-10-for-x86_64-baseos-rpms

If the "pkcs11-provider" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have the "pkcs11-provider" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install pkcs11-provider
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the use of multifactor authentication (MFA), the ease of access to privileged functions is greatly increased. MFA requires using two or more factors to achieve authentication. A privileged account is defined as an information system account with authorizations of a privileged user. The DoW common access card (CAC) with DoW-approved PKI is an example of MFA.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000105-GPOS-00052, SRG-OS-000375-GPOS-00160, SRG-OS-000377-GPOS-00162

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000765**: Implement multifactor authentication for access to privileged accounts.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (1) · Rev 4: IA-2 (1) · Rev 3: IA-2 (1)
- **CCI-004046**: Implement multi-factor authentication for local; network; and/or remote access to privileged accounts; and/or non-privileged accounts such that one of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system gaining access.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (6) (a) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001954**: Electronically verify Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (12) · Rev 4: IA-2 (12) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281006 · RHEL-10-200740 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must have the "gnutls-utils" package installed.

| Field | Value |

| Rule ID | `SV-281006r1195397_rule` |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "gnutls-utils" package installed.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | gnutls-utils | Installed |

**How it works:** On RHEL, remove packages with 'dnf remove <pkg>' and verify with 'rpm -q <pkg>' (expect 'package <pkg> is not installed'). Watch for dependency cascades in the dnf transaction summary before confirming.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 has the "gnutls-utils" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list --installed gnutls-utils
Installed Packages
gnutls-utils.x86_64                         3.8.9-9.el10_0.14                         @rhel-10-for-x86_64-appstream-rpms

If the "gnutls-utils" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have the "gnutls-utils" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install gnutls-utils
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** "GnuTLS" is a secure communications library implementing the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL), Transport Layer Security (TLS), and Datagram TLS (DTLS) protocols and technologies around them. It provides a simple C language application programming interface (API) to access the secure communications protocols as well as APIs to parse and write X.509, PKCS #12, OpenPGP, and other required structures. This package contains command line TLS client and server and certificate manipulation tools.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-281007 · RHEL-10-300000 · CAT I: RHEL 10 must have the "crypto-policies" package installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281007r1195399_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000396-GPOS-00176 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140) |
| CCI | CCI-002450, CCI-002890, CCI-003123 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-13 b, MA-4 (6) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-13, MA-4 (6) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "crypto-policies" package installed.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | dnf | crypto-policies | Installed |

**How it works:** RHEL centralizes crypto settings in system-wide crypto policies: 'fips-mode-setup --enable' (RHEL 8) or 'fips=1' on the kernel command line at install time (RHEL 9/10), then 'update-crypto-policies --set FIPS'. Back-end files under /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ (openssh, opensslcnf, bind, gnutls and others) are generated from the policy, and individual services such as sshd must be pointed at them rather than hard-coding algorithms. Verify with 'fips-mode-setup --check' and 'update-crypto-policies --show'.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 has the "crypto-policies" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list --installed crypto-policies
Installed Packages
crypto-policies.noarch                  20250214-1.gitfd9b9b9.el10_0.1                   @rhel-10-for-x86_64-baseos-rpms

If the "crypto-policies" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have the "crypto-policies" package installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y install crypto-policies
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Centralized cryptographic policies simplify applying secure ciphers across an operating system and the applications that run on that operating system. Use of weak or untested encryption algorithms undermines the purposes of using encryption to protect data.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000396-GPOS-00176, SRG-OS-000393-GPOS-00173, SRG-OS-000394-GPOS-00174

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002450**: Implement organization-defined types of cryptography for each specified cryptography use.  
  Rev 5: SC-13 b · Rev 4: SC-13 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002890**: Implement organization-defined cryptographic mechanisms to protect the integrity of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic communications.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (6) · Rev 4: MA-4 (6) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-003123**: Implement organization-defined cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic communications.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (6) · Rev 4: MA-4 (6) · Rev 3: n/a

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** RHEL centralizes crypto settings in system-wide crypto policies: 'fips-mode-setup --enable' (RHEL 8) or 'fips=1' on the kernel command line at install time (RHEL 9/10), then 'update-crypto-policies --set FIPS'. Back-end files under /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ (openssh, opensslcnf, bind, gnutls and others) are generated from the policy, and individual services such as sshd must be pointed at them rather than hard-coding algorithms. Verify with 'fips-mode-setup --check' and 'update-crypto-policies --show'.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is set to use a FIPS 140-3-compliant systemwide cryptographic policy.

Verify the current systemwide crypto-policy with the following command:

$ update-crypto-policies --show
FIPS

If the systemwide crypto-policy is not set to "FIPS", this is a finding.

Verify the current minimum crypto-policy configuration with the following commands:

$ sudo grep -E 'rsa_size|hash' /etc/crypto-policies/state/CURRENT.pol
hash = SHA2-256 SHA2-384 SHA2-512 SHA2-224 SHA3-256 SHA3-384 SHA3-512 SHAKE-256
min_rsa_size = 2048

If the "hash" values do not include at least the following FIPS 140-3-compliant algorithms, this is a finding:

"SHA2-256 SHA2-384 SHA2-512 SHA2-224 SHA3-256 SHA3-384 SHA3-512 SHAKE-256"

If any algorithms include "SHA1" or a hash value less than "224", this is a finding.

If the "min_rsa_size" is not set to a value of at least "2048", this is a finding.

If these commands do not return any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use a FIPS 140-3-compliant systemwide cryptographic policy.

Set the systemwide crypto-policy to FIPS with the following command:

$ sudo update-crypto-policies --set FIPS
Setting system policy to FIPS

Note: Systemwide crypto-policies are applied on application startup. It is recommended to restart the system for the change of policies to fully take place.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Centralized cryptographic policies simplify applying secure ciphers across an operating system and the applications that run on that operating system. Use of weak or untested encryption algorithms undermines the purposes of using encryption to protect data.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000033-GPOS-00014, SRG-OS-000396-GPOS-00176, SRG-OS-000393-GPOS-00173, SRG-OS-000394-GPOS-00174

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000068**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (2) · Rev 4: AC-17 (2) · Rev 3: AC-17 (2)
- **CCI-002450**: Implement organization-defined types of cryptography for each specified cryptography use.  
  Rev 5: SC-13 b · Rev 4: SC-13 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002890**: Implement organization-defined cryptographic mechanisms to protect the integrity of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic communications.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (6) · Rev 4: MA-4 (6) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-003123**: Implement organization-defined cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic communications.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (6) · Rev 4: MA-4 (6) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281010 · RHEL-10-300030 · CAT I: RHEL 10 must be configured so that Secure Shell (SSH) clients use only DoW-approved encryption ciphers employing FIPS 140-3-validated cryptographic hash algorithms to protect the confidentiality of SSH client connections.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281010r1273569_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000033-GPOS-00014 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140), SSH Remote Administration |
| CCI | CCI-000068, CCI-000877, CCI-001453, CCI-002890, CCI-003123, CCI-002418 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-17 (2), MA-4 c, MA-4 (6), SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-17 (2), MA-4 c, MA-4 (6), SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-17 (2), MA-4 c |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that Secure Shell (SSH) clients use only DoW-approved encryption ciphers employing FIPS 140-3-validated cryptographic hash algorithms to protect the confidentiality of SSH client connections.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** RHEL centralizes crypto settings in system-wide crypto policies: 'fips-mode-setup --enable' (RHEL 8) or 'fips=1' on the kernel command line at install time (RHEL 9/10), then 'update-crypto-policies --set FIPS'. Back-end files under /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ (openssh, opensslcnf, bind, gnutls and others) are generated from the policy, and individual services such as sshd must be pointed at them rather than hard-coding algorithms. Verify with 'fips-mode-setup --check' and 'update-crypto-policies --show'.

**Also related (SSH Remote Administration):** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 SSH clients are configured to use only ciphers employing FIPS 140-3-approved algorithms.

To verify the ciphers in the systemwide SSH configuration file, use the following command:

$ sudo grep -i Ciphers /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/openssh.config
Ciphers aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes256-ctr,aes128-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-ctr

If the cipher entries in the "openssh.config" file have any ciphers other than "aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes256-ctr,aes128-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-ctr", or they are missing or commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 SSH clients to use only ciphers employing FIPS 140-3-approved algorithms.

Reinstall crypto-policies with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y reinstall crypto-policies

Set the crypto-policy to FIPS with the following command:

$ sudo update-crypto-policies --set FIPS
Setting system policy to FIPS

Note: Systemwide crypto policies are applied on application startup. It is recommended to restart the system for the change of policies to fully take place.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without cryptographic integrity protections, information can be altered by unauthorized users without detection.

Remote access (e.g., Remote Desktop Protocol [RDP]) is access to DoW nonpublic information systems by an authorized user (or an information system) communicating through an external, nonorganizational-controlled network. Remote access methods include, for example, dial-up, broadband, and wireless.

Cryptographic mechanisms used for protecting the integrity of information include, for example, signed hash functions that use asymmetric cryptography. This enables distribution of the public key to verify the hash information while maintaining the confidentiality of the secret key used to generate the hash.

RHEL 10 incorporates systemwide crypto policies by default. The SSH configuration file has no effect on the ciphers, MACs, or algorithms unless specifically defined in the "/etc/sysconfig/sshd" file. The employed algorithms can be viewed in the "/etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/openssh.config" file.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000033-GPOS-00014, SRG-OS-000125-GPOS-00065, SRG-OS-000250-GPOS-00093, SRG-OS-000393-GPOS-00173, SRG-OS-000394-GPOS-00174, SRG-OS-000423-GPOS-00187

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption; T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000068**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (2) · Rev 4: AC-17 (2) · Rev 3: AC-17 (2)
- **CCI-000877**: Employ strong authentication in the establishment of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 c · Rev 4: MA-4 c · Rev 3: MA-4 c
- **CCI-001453**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the integrity of remote access sessions.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (2) · Rev 4: AC-17 (2) · Rev 3: AC-17 (2)
- **CCI-002890**: Implement organization-defined cryptographic mechanisms to protect the integrity of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic communications.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (6) · Rev 4: MA-4 (6) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-003123**: Implement organization-defined cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic communications.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (6) · Rev 4: MA-4 (6) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002418**: Protect the confidentiality and/or integrity of transmitted information.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 · Rev 4: SC-8 · Rev 3: n/a

Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 SSH servers are configured to use only MACs employing FIPS 140-3-approved algorithms with the following command:

$ sudo grep -i MACs /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/opensshserver.config
MACs hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256,hmac-sha2-512

If the MACs entries in the "opensshserver.config" file have any hashes other than "hmac-sha2-512" and "hmac-sha2-256", the order differs from the example above, or they are missing or commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 SSH servers to use only MACs employing FIPS 140-3-approved algorithms.

Reinstall crypto-policies with the following command:

$ sudo dnf -y reinstall crypto-policies

Set the crypto-policy to FIPS with the following command:

$ sudo update-crypto-policies --set FIPS
Setting system policy to FIPS

Note: Systemwide crypto policies are applied on application startup. It is recommended to restart the system for the change of policies to fully take place.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without cryptographic integrity protections, information can be altered by unauthorized users without detection.

Remote access (e.g., Remote Desktop Protocol [RDP]) is access to DoW nonpublic information systems by an authorized user (or an information system) communicating through an external, nonorganization-controlled network. Remote access methods include, for example, dial-up, broadband, and wireless.

Cryptographic mechanisms used for protecting the integrity of information include, for example, signed hash functions using asymmetric cryptography enabling distribution of the public key to verify the hash information while maintaining the confidentiality of the secret key used to generate the hash.

RHEL 10 incorporates systemwide crypto policies by default. The SSH configuration file has no effect on the ciphers, MACs, or algorithms unless specifically defined in the "/etc/sysconfig/sshd" file. The employed algorithms can be viewed in the "/etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/opensshserver.config" file.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000125-GPOS-00065, SRG-OS-000250-GPOS-00093

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption; T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000877**: Employ strong authentication in the establishment of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 c · Rev 4: MA-4 c · Rev 3: MA-4 c
- **CCI-001453**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the integrity of remote access sessions.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (2) · Rev 4: AC-17 (2) · Rev 3: AC-17 (2)
