### V-281073 · RHEL-10-400280 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured so that a sticky bit is set on all public directories.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281073r1273578_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-001090 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-4 |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that a sticky bit is set on all public directories.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | a+t [World-Writable Directory] |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that all world-writable directories have the sticky bit set with the following command:

$ sudo find / -type d \( -perm -0002 -a ! -perm -1000 \) -print 2>/dev/null
drwxrwxrwt 7 root root 4096 Jul 26 11:19 /tmp

If any of the returned directories are world-writable and do not have the sticky bit set, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that all world-writable directories have the sticky bit set to prevent unauthorized and unintended information transferred via shared system resources.

Set the sticky bit on all world-writable directories using the following command (replace "[World-Writable Directory]" with any directory path missing the sticky bit):

$ chmod a+t [World-Writable Directory]
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Preventing unauthorized information transfers mitigates the risk of information, including encrypted representations of information, produced by the actions of prior users/roles (or the actions of processes acting on behalf of prior users/roles) from being available to any current users/roles (or current processes) that obtain access to shared system resources (e.g., registers, main memory, hard disks) after those resources have been released back to information systems. The control of information in shared resources is also commonly referred to as object reuse and residual information protection.

This requirement generally applies to the design of an information technology product, but it can also apply to the configuration of information system components that are, or use, such products. This can be verified by acceptance/validation processes in DoW or other government agencies.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001090**: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.  
  Rev 5: SC-4 · Rev 4: SC-4 · Rev 3: SC-4

It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chgrp | <group> <file> |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. **Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that all local files and directories have a valid group with the following command:

$ df --local -P | awk {'if (NR!=1) print $6'} | sudo xargs -I '{}' find '{}' -xdev -nogroup

If any files on the system do not have an assigned group, this is a finding.
```

```text

$ sudo chgrp <group> <file>
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Files without a valid group owner may be unintentionally inherited if a group is assigned the same group identifier (GID) as the GID of the files without a valid group owner.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**Why it matters:** The security diary is only useful if nobody can secretly edit or tear pages out of it. This rule locks down who can read or change the logs and the tools that manage them. It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chown | root [audit_tool] |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, audit logs live under /var/log/audit/ (mode 0600 or 0640, owned by root, group per log_group). Audit tools are /sbin/auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, rsyslogd and augenrules (mode 0755, owned by root). '-e 2' at the end of the rules makes the configuration immutable until reboot, and '--loginuid-immutable' prevents processes from changing their audit login UID.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 audit tools are owned by "root" with the following command:

$ sudo stat -c "%U %n" /sbin/auditctl /sbin/aureport /sbin/ausearch /sbin/auditd /sbin/rsyslogd /sbin/augenrules
root /sbin/auditctl
root /sbin/aureport
root /sbin/ausearch
root /sbin/auditd
root /sbin/rsyslogd
root /sbin/augenrules

If any audit tools do not have an owner of "root", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that the audit tools are owned by "root" by running the following command:

$ sudo chown root [audit_tool]

Replace "[audit_tool]" with each audit tool not owned by "root".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Protecting audit information also includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Therefore, protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.

RHEL 10 systems providing tools to interface with audit information will leverage user permissions and roles identifying the user accessing the tools, and the corresponding rights the user enjoys, to make access decisions regarding the access to audit tools.

Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000256-GPOS-00097, SRG-OS-000257-GPOS-00098, SRG-OS-000258-GPOS-00099

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001493**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized access.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-001494**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized modification.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-001495**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized deletion.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

### V-281079 · RHEL-10-400310 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must set the umask value to "077" for all local interactive user accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281079r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must set the umask value to "077" for all local interactive user accounts.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *umask*: The default permission setting given to newly created files.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 sets the default umask for all local interactive users to "077".

Identify the locations of all local interactive user home directories by looking at the "/etc/passwd" file.

Check all local interactive user initialization files for interactive users with the following command:

Note: The example is for a system that is configured to create users' home directories in the "/home" directory.

$ sudo find /home -maxdepth 2 -type f -name ".[^.]*" -exec grep -iH -d skip --exclude=.bash_history umask {} \;
/home/disauser/.bash_history:grep -i umask /etc/bashrc /etc/csh.cshrc /etc/profile
/home/disauser/.bash_history:grep -i umask /etc/login.defs

If any local interactive user initialization files are found to have a umask statement that sets a value less restrictive than "077", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to set the umask value for all local interactive user accounts to "077".

Remove the umask statement from all local interactive users' initialization files.

If the account is for an application, the requirement for a umask less restrictive than "077" can be documented with the information system security officer. However, the user agreement for access to the account must specify that the local interactive user must log in to their account first and then switch the user to the application account with the correct option to gain the account's environment variables.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The umask controls the default access mode assigned to newly created files. A umask of "077" limits new files to mode 600 or less permissive. Although umask can be represented as a four-digit number, the first digit representing special access modes is typically ignored or required to be "0". This requirement applies to the globally configured system defaults and the local interactive user defaults for each account on the system.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/bashrc | umask | 077 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 "umask" setting is configured correctly in the "/etc/bashrc" file with the following command:

Note: If the value of the "umask" parameter is set to "000" in the "/etc/bashrc" file, the Severity is raised to a CAT I.

$ sudo grep umask /etc/bashrc
[ `umask` -eq 0 ] && umask 077

If the value for the "umask" parameter is not "077", or the "umask" parameter is missing or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to define default permissions for all authenticated users using the bash shell.

Add or edit the lines for the "umask" parameter in the "/etc/bashrc" file to "077":

umask 077
```

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *umask*: The default permission setting given to newly created files.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/profile | umask | 077 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the RHEL 10 "umask" setting is configured correctly in the "/etc/profile" file with the following command:

Note: If the value of the "umask" parameter is set to "000" in the "/etc/profile" file, the Severity is raised to a CAT I.

$ sudo grep umask /etc/profile
umask 077

If the value for the "umask" parameter is not "077", or the "umask" parameter is missing or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to define default permissions for all authenticated users in such a way that the user can read and modify only their own files.

Add or edit the lines for the "umask" parameter in the "/etc/profile" file to "077":

umask 077
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "umask" controls the default access mode assigned to newly created files. A "umask" of "077" limits new files to mode "600" or less permissive. "Although umask" can be represented as a four-digit number, the first digit representing special access modes is typically ignored or required to be "0".

This requirement applies to the globally configured system defaults and the local interactive user defaults for each account on the system.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281085 · RHEL-10-400340 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enforce mode "0600" or less permissive for Secure Shell (SSH) private host key files.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281085r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | SSH Remote Administration, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce mode "0600" or less permissive for Secure Shell (SSH) private host key files.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | 0600 /etc/ssh/ssh_host*key |  |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces mode "0600" for SSH private host key files with the following command:

$ sudo stat -c "%a %n" /etc/ssh/*_key
600 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ecdsa_key
600 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key
600 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key

If any private host key file has a mode more permissive than "0600", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce mode "0600" for SSH private host key files with the following command:

$ sudo chmod 0600 /etc/ssh/ssh_host*key

Restart the SSH daemon for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If an unauthorized user obtains the private SSH host key file, the host could be impersonated.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

| Topic | File & Directory Permissions, Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce "root" group ownership of the "/boot/grub2/grub.cfg" file.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chgrp | root /boot/grub2/grub.cfg |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Also related (Boot Process & Console Security):** On RHEL, set the GRUB2 superuser password with 'grub2-setpassword' (stored hashed in /boot/grub2/user.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/user.cfg) and set a unique superuser name in /etc/grub.d/01_users. Rescue and emergency modes must require root authentication (sulogin in rescue.service and emergency.service). Mask Ctrl-Alt-Del with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none' in systemd's system.conf. Mask debug-shell. kdump is disabled unless it's needed.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces group ownership of the "/boot/grub2/grub.cfg" file with the following command:

$ sudo stat -c "%G %n" /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
root /boot/grub2/grub.cfg

If the "/boot/grub2/grub.cfg" file does not have a group owner of "root", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce group ownership of the "/boot/grub2/grub.cfg" file.

Change the group owner of the file "/boot/grub2/grub.cfg" to "root" by running the following command:

$ sudo chgrp root /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "root" group is a highly privileged group. Furthermore, the group owner of this file should not have any access privileges anyway.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid; T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.

### V-281088 · RHEL-10-400355 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent device files from being interpreted on file systems that contain user home directories.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281088r1165619_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management, File System Layout & Mount Options |
| CCI | CCI-001764 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent device files from being interpreted on file systems that contain user home directories.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that "/home" is mounted with the "nodev" option with the following command:

Note: If a separate file system has not been created for the user home directories (user home directories are mounted under "/"), this is automatically a finding, as the "nodev" option cannot be used on the "/" system.

$ mount | grep /home
/dev/mapper/luks-ca2261ed-7b00-4b7b-84cd-8cd6d8fa4b28 on /home type xfs (rw,nodev,nosuid,noexec,seclabel)

If the "/home" file system is mounted without the "nodev" option, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent device files from being interpreted on file systems that contain user home directories.

Modify "/etc/fstab" to use the "nodev" option on the "/home" directory.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nodev" mount option causes the system to not interpret character or block special devices. Executing character or block special devices from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

The only legitimate location for device files is the "/dev" directory located on the root partition, with the exception of chroot jails if implemented.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that "/home" is mounted with the "nosuid" option with the following command:

Note: If a separate file system has not been created for the user home directories (user home directories are mounted under "/"), this is automatically a finding, as the "nosuid" option cannot be used on the "/" system.

$ mount | grep /home
/dev/mapper/luks-ca2261ed-7b00-4b7b-84cd-8cd6d8fa4b28 on /home type xfs (rw,nodev,nosuid,noexec,seclabel)

If the "/home" file system is mounted without the "nosuid" option, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent files with the "setuid" and "setgid" bit set from being executed on file systems that contain user home directories.

Modify "/etc/fstab" to use the "nosuid" option on the "/home" directory.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nosuid" mount option causes the system to not execute "setuid" and "setgid" files with owner privileges. This option must be used for mounting any file system not containing approved "setuid" and "setguid" files. Executing files from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent code from being executed on file systems that contain user home directories.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

```text

Note: If a separate file system has not been created for the user home directories (user home directories are mounted under "/"), this is automatically a finding, as the "noexec" option cannot be used on the "/" system.

$ mount | grep /home
/dev/mapper/luks-ca2261ed-7b00-4b7b-84cd-8cd6d8fa4b28 on /home type xfs (rw,nodev,nosuid,noexec,seclabel)

If the "/home" file system is mounted without the "noexec" option, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent code from being executed on file systems that contain user home directories.

Modify "/etc/fstab" to use the "noexec" option on the "/home" directory.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "noexec" mount option causes the system to not execute binary files. This option must be used for mounting any file system not containing approved binary files, as they may be incompatible. Executing files from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

### V-281091 · RHEL-10-400400 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must mount "/var/log/audit" with the "nodev" option.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281091r1165628_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154 |
| Topic | File System Layout & Mount Options, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-001764 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must mount "/var/log/audit" with the "nodev" option.

**Why it matters:** The computer's storage is divided into separate sections, like rooms in a house. This rule keeps certain rooms separate so one can't overflow into the others, and marks rooms such as the "temporary storage" area as places where programs aren't allowed to run. It's like a garage where you can store things but nobody is allowed to live.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that "/var/log/audit" is mounted with the "nodev" option:

$ mount | grep /var/log/audit
/dev/mapper/luks-4e45e1ad-5337-42c4-a19f-ee12ccc1d502 on /var/log/audit type xfs (rw,nodev,nosuid,noexec,seclabel)

If the "/var/log/audit" file system is mounted without the "nodev" option, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to mount "/var/log/audit" with the "nodev" option.

Modify "/etc/fstab" to use the "nodev" option on the "/var/log/audit" directory.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nodev" mount option causes the system to not interpret character or block special devices. Executing character or block special devices from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

The only legitimate location for device files is the "/dev" directory located on the root partition, with the exception of chroot jails if implemented.

**Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281094 · RHEL-10-400450 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enforce a mode of "0755" or less permissive for audit tools.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281094r1165637_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000256-GPOS-00097 |
| Topic | Audit Log & Tool Protection, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-001493, CCI-001494, CCI-001495 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-9 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-9 |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce a mode of "0755" or less permissive for audit tools.

**Why it matters:** The security diary is only useful if nobody can secretly edit or tear pages out of it. This rule locks down who can read or change the logs and the tools that manage them. It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | 0755 [audit_tool] |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, audit logs live under /var/log/audit/ (mode 0600 or 0640, owned by root, group per log_group). Audit tools are /sbin/auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, rsyslogd and augenrules (mode 0755, owned by root). '-e 2' at the end of the rules makes the configuration immutable until reboot, and '--loginuid-immutable' prevents processes from changing their audit login UID.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that the audit tools have a mode of "0755" or less with the following command:

$ stat -c "%a %n" /sbin/auditctl /sbin/aureport /sbin/ausearch /sbin/auditd /sbin/rsyslogd /sbin/augenrules
755 /sbin/auditctl
755 /sbin/aureport
755 /sbin/ausearch
755 /sbin/auditd
755 /sbin/rsyslogd
755 /sbin/augenrules

If any of the audit tool files have a mode more permissive than "0755", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that the audit tools to have a mode of "0755" by running the following command:

$ sudo chmod 0755 [audit_tool]

Replace "[audit_tool]" with each audit tool that has a mode more permissive than "0755".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Protecting audit information also includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Therefore, protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.

RHEL 10 systems providing tools to interface with audit information will leverage user permissions and roles identifying the user accessing the tools, and the corresponding rights the user enjoys, to make access decisions regarding the access to audit tools.

Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000256-GPOS-00097, SRG-OS-000257-GPOS-00098, SRG-OS-000258-GPOS-00099

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001493**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized access.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-001494**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized modification.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-001495**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized deletion.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prohibit local initialization files from executing world-writable programs.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | 0755 <file> |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 local initialization files do not execute world-writable programs with the following command:

Note: The example will be for a system that is configured to create user home directories in the "/home" directory.

$ sudo find /home -perm -002 -type f -name ".[^.]*" -exec ls -ld {} \;

If any local initialization files are found to reference world-writable files, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that local initialization files do not execute world-writable programs with the following command:

$ sudo chmod 0755 <file>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If user startup files execute world-writable programs, especially in unprotected directories, they could be maliciously modified to destroy user files or otherwise compromise the system at the user level. If the system is compromised at the user level, it is easier to elevate privileges to eventually compromise the system at the root and network level.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-281096 · RHEL-10-500000 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enable the systemd-journald service.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281096r1165643_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000269-GPOS-00103 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-001665 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-24 |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enable the systemd-journald service.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service | systemd | systemd-journald | enable (now) |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, admin_space_left(_action), disk_full_action, disk_error_action, max_log_file(_action), action_mail_acct). Off-loading uses rsyslog (omfwd with TLS via gtls/ossl stream drivers) or the audisp-remote / audit 'remote' plugin. Put /var/log/audit on its own partition so it can't starve the root file system. Restart with 'service auditd restart', because systemctl is blocked for auditd.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enables the systemd-journald service with the following command:

$ systemctl is-active systemd-journald
active

If the systemd-journald service is not active, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enable the systemd-journald service.

To enable the systemd-journald service, run the following command:

$ sudo systemctl enable --now systemd-journald
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** In the event of a system failure, RHEL 10 must preserve any information necessary to determine cause of failure and return to operations with least disruption to system processes.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001665**: Preserve organization-defined system state information in the event of a system failure.  
  Rev 5: SC-24 · Rev 4: SC-24 · Rev 3: SC-24

### V-281097 · RHEL-10-500005 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enable auditing of processes that start prior to the audit daemon.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281097r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enable auditing of processes that start prior to the audit daemon.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *Boot loader (GRUB)*: The small program that starts the operating system when the computer powers on.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/default/grub | GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX | "audit=1" |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that GRUB 2 enables auditing of processes that start prior to the audit daemon with the following commands:

Check that the current GRUB 2 configuration enables auditing:

$ sudo grubby --info=ALL | grep args | grep -v 'audit=1'

If any output is returned, this is a finding.

Check that auditing is enabled by default to persist in kernel updates:

$ sudo grep audit /etc/default/grub
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="audit=1"

If "audit" is not set to "1", is missing, or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enable auditing of processes that start prior to the audit daemon with the following command:

$ sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="audit=1"

Add or modify the following line in "/etc/default/grub" to ensure the configuration survives kernel updates:

GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="audit=1"
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the capability to generate audit records, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

If auditing is enabled late in the startup process, the actions of some startup processes may not be audited. Some audit systems also maintain state information available only if auditing is enabled before a given process is created.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281100 · RHEL-10-500020 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must log username information when unsuccessful login attempts occur.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281100r1165655_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000044 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must log username information when unsuccessful login attempts occur.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 "/etc/security/faillock.conf" is configured to log username information when unsuccessful login attempts occur with the following command:

$ sudo grep audit /etc/security/faillock.conf
audit

If the "audit" option is not set, is missing, or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to log username information when unsuccessful login attempts occur.

Enable the feature using the following command:

$ sudo authselect enable-feature with-faillock

Add/modify the "/etc/security/faillock.conf" file to match the following line:

audit
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without auditing of these events, it may be harder or impossible to identify what an attacker did after an attack.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a

```text
$ sudo chmod 0600 /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules
$ sudo chmod 0640 /etc/audit/rules.d/[customrulesfile].rules
$ sudo chmod 0640 /etc/audit/auditd.conf
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the capability to restrict the roles and individuals that can select which events are audited, unauthorized personnel may be able to prevent the auditing of critical events. Misconfigured audits may degrade the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfigured audits may also make it more difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000171**: Allow organization-defined personnel or roles to select the event types that are to be logged by specific components of the system.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 b · Rev 4: AU-12 b · Rev 3: AU-12 b

### V-281102 · RHEL-10-500030 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must allocate an "audit_backlog_limit" of sufficient size to capture processes that start prior to the audit daemon.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281102r1195414_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-001464, CCI-001849, CCI-002884, CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-14 (1), AU-4, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-14 (1), AU-4, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-14 (1), AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must allocate an "audit_backlog_limit" of sufficient size to capture processes that start prior to the audit daemon.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 allocates a sufficient "audit_backlog_limit" to capture processes that start prior to the audit daemon with the following command:

$ grep -oP 'audit_backlog_limit=\K[0-9]+' /proc/cmdline
8192

If the command returns any outputs, and "audit_backlog_limit" is less than "8192", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to allocate sufficient "audit_backlog_limit" to capture processes that start prior to the audit daemon with the following command:

$ sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=audit_backlog_limit=8192

The setting will be applied on reboot.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the capability to generate audit records, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

If auditing is enabled late in the startup process, the actions of some startup processes may not be audited. Some audit systems also maintain state information only available if auditing is enabled before a given process is created.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

Allocating an "audit_backlog_limit" of sufficient size is critical in maintaining a stable boot process. With an insufficient limit allocated, the system is susceptible to boot failures and crashes.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000254-GPOS-00095, SRG-OS-000341-GPOS-00132, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000169**: Provide audit record generation capability for the event types the system is capable of auditing as defined in AU-2 a on organization-defined information system components.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a
- **CCI-001464**: Initiates session audits automatically at system start-up.  
  Rev 5: AU-14 (1) · Rev 4: AU-14 (1) · Rev 3: AU-14 (1)
- **CCI-001849**: Allocate audit log storage capacity to accommodate organization-defined audit log retention requirements.  
  Rev 5: AU-4 · Rev 4: AU-4 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c
