### V-281138 · RHEL-10-500520 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the ssh-agent command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281138r1197227_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015 |
| Topic | SSH Remote Administration, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-002884, CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the ssh-agent command.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/ssh-agent -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-ssh |  |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to audit the execution of the "ssh-agent" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep ssh-agent
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/usr/bin/ssh-agent -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=privileged-ssh

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records upon successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the "ssh-agent" command by adding or updating the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/ssh-agent -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-ssh

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each system call made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use system call rules only when absolutely necessary because these affect performance. More rules lead to poorer performance. The performance can be helped, however, by combining system calls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000169**: Provide audit record generation capability for the event types the system is capable of auditing as defined in AU-2 a on organization-defined information system components.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-281140 · RHEL-10-500540 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the "su" command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281140r1197229_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-000172, CCI-002884, CCI-004188 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-12 c, MA-4 (1) (a), MA-3 (5) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-12 c, MA-4 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the "su" command.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to audit the execution of the "su" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep '/usr/bin/su\b'
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/usr/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=privileged-priv_change

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records upon successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the "su" command by adding or updating the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/su -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-priv_change

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each system call made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use system call rules only when absolutely necessary because these affect performance. More rules lead to poorer performance. The performance can be helped, however, by combining system calls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000064-GPOS-00033, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000755-GPOS-00220

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user.   Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a

UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-281142 · RHEL-10-500560 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the "sudoedit" command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281142r1197231_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-002884, CCI-000172, CCI-004188 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c, MA-3 (5) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the "sudoedit" command.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/sudoedit -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k priv_cmd |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to audit the execution of the "sudoedit" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep /usr/bin/sudoedit
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/usr/bin/sudoedit -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=priv_cmd

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records upon successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the "sudoedit" command by adding or updating the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/bin/sudoedit -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k priv_cmd

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each system call made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use system call rules only when absolutely necessary because these affect performance. More rules lead to poorer performance. The performance can be helped, however, by combining system calls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000755-GPOS-00220

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000169**: Provide audit record generation capability for the event types the system is capable of auditing as defined in AU-2 a on organization-defined information system components.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the "unix_chkpwd" command.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/sbin/unix_chkpwd -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-unix-update |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to audit the execution of the "unix_chkpwd" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep unix_chkpwd
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/usr/sbin/unix_chkpwd -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=privileged-unix-update

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records upon successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the "unix_chkpwd" command by adding or updating the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/sbin/unix_chkpwd -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-unix-update

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each system call made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use system call rules only when absolutely necessary because these affect performance. More rules lead to poorer performance. The performance can be helped, however, by combining system calls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215

### V-281146 · RHEL-10-500600 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the "usermod" command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281146r1197235_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-002884, CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for successful and unsuccessful uses of the "usermod" command.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F path=/usr/sbin/usermod -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-usermod |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to audit the execution of the "usermod" command with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep usermod
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/usr/sbin/usermod -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=privileged-usermod

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records upon successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the "usermod" command by adding or updating the following rule in "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F path=/usr/sbin/usermod -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k privileged-usermod

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each system call made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use system call rules only when absolutely necessary because these affect performance. More rules lead to poorer performance. The performance can be helped, however, by combining system calls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000169**: Provide audit record generation capability for the event types the system is capable of auditing as defined in AU-2 a on organization-defined information system components.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.

### V-281154 · RHEL-10-500680 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/sudoers".

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281154r1273585_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000004-GPOS-00004 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000018, CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-000015, CCI-002884, CCI-000172, CCI-001403, CCI-001404, CCI-001405, CCI-002130 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (4), AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (4), AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (4), AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/sudoers".

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 generates audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/sudoers" with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep '/etc/sudoers[^.]'
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=identity

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/sudoers".

Add or update the following file system rule to "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=identity

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The actions taken by system administrators must be audited to keep a record of what was executed on the system, as well as for accountability purposes. Editing the "sudoers" file may be sign of an attacker trying to establish persistent methods to a system. Auditing the editing of the "sudoers" files mitigates this risk.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000004-GPOS-00004, SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000304-GPOS-00121, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000239-GPOS-00089, SRG-OS-000240-GPOS-00090, SRG-OS-000241-GPOS-00091, SRG-OS-000303-GPOS-00120, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000476-GPOS-00221

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-281155 · RHEL-10-500690 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect the "/etc/sudoers.d/" directory.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281155r1273586_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000004-GPOS-00004 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000018, CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-000015, CCI-002884, CCI-000172, CCI-001403, CCI-001404, CCI-001405, CCI-002130 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (4), AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (4), AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (4), AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect the "/etc/sudoers.d/" directory.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 generates audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/sudoers.d/" with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep /etc/sudoers.d
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=identity

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/sudoers.d/".

Add or update the following file system rule to "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=identity

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The actions taken by system administrators must be audited to keep a record of what was executed on the system, as well as for accountability purposes. Editing the "sudoers" file may be a sign of an attacker trying to establish persistent methods to a system. Auditing the editing of the "sudoers" files mitigates this risk.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000004-GPOS-00004, SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000304-GPOS-00121, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000239-GPOS-00089, SRG-OS-000240-GPOS-00090, SRG-OS-000241-GPOS-00091, SRG-OS-000303-GPOS-00120, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000476-GPOS-00221

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/group".

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/group -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/group -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 generates audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/group" with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | egrep '(/etc/group)'
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/group -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/group -F perm=wa -F key=identity

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/group".

Add or update the following file system rule to "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/group -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/group -F perm=wa -F key=identity

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** In addition to auditing new user and group accounts, these watches will alert the system administrator(s) to any modifications. Any unexpected users, groups, or modifications must be investigated for legitimacy.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000004-GPOS-00004, SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000304-GPOS-00121, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000239-GPOS-00089, SRG-OS-000240-GPOS-00090, SRG-OS-000241-GPOS-00091, SRG-OS-000303-GPOS-00120, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000476-GPOS-00221

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

### V-281158 · RHEL-10-500720 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/security/opasswd".

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281158r1273587_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000004-GPOS-00004 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000018, CCI-000130, CCI-000135, CCI-000169, CCI-000015, CCI-002884, CCI-000172, CCI-001403, CCI-001404, CCI-001405, CCI-002130 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (4), AU-3 a, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (4), AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), MA-4 (1) (a), AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (4), AU-3, AU-3 (1), AU-12 a, AC-2 (1), AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/etc/security/opasswd".

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/identity.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/security/opasswd -F perm=wa -k identity |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/identity.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/security/opasswd -F perm=wa -k identity |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 generates audit records for modifications to "/etc/security/opasswd" with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep '/etc/security/opasswd'

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/security/opasswd -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/security/opasswd -F perm=wa -F key=identity

If the command does not return these lines, or the lines are commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records for all modifications to "/etc/security/opasswd" by adding or updating the following rules in "/etc/audit/rules.d/identity.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/etc/security/opasswd -F perm=wa -k identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/etc/security/opasswd -F perm=wa -k identity

To load the rules to the kernel immediately, use the following command:

$ sudo augenrules --load
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** In addition to auditing new user and group accounts, these watches will alert the system administrator(s) to any modifications. Any unexpected users, groups, or modifications should be investigated for legitimacy.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000004-GPOS-00004, SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000304-GPOS-00121, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000239-GPOS-00089, SRG-OS-000240-GPOS-00090, SRG-OS-000241-GPOS-00091, SRG-OS-000303-GPOS-00120, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000476-GPOS-00221

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**

| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/var/log/faillock -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/var/log/faillock -F perm=wa -F key=identity |  |

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 generates audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/var/log/faillock" with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep /var/log/faillock
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/var/log/faillock -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/var/log/faillock -F perm=wa -F key=identity

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/var/log/faillock".

Add or update the following file system rule to "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -F path=/var/log/faillock -F perm=wa -F key=identity
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/var/log/faillock -F perm=wa -F key=identity

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214, SRG-OS-000473-GPOS-00218

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for all account creations, modifications, disabling, and termination events that affect "/var/log/lastlog".

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |

| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/var/log/lastlog -F perm=wa -F key=logins |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=/var/log/lastlog -F perm=wa -F key=logins

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records that are specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account that is being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each syscall made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use syscall rules only when absolutely necessary because these affect performance. More rules lead to poorer performance. The performance can be helped, however, by combining syscalls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000064-GPOS-00033, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000458-GPOS-00203

The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000169**: Provide audit record generation capability for the event types the system is capable of auditing as defined in AU-2 a on organization-defined information system components.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate audit records for all uses of the "rename", "unlink", "rmdir", "renameat", "renameat2", and "unlinkat" system calls.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S rename,unlink,rmdir,renameat,renameat2,unlinkat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete |  |
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S rename,unlink,rmdir,renameat,renameat2,unlinkat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to audit successful/unsuccessful attempts to use the "rename", "unlink", "rmdir", "renameat", "renameat2", and "unlinkat" system calls with the following command:

$ sudo auditctl -l | grep 'rename\|unlink\|rmdir'
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S rename,unlink,rmdir,renameat,renameat2,unlinkat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S rename,unlink,rmdir,renameat,renameat2,unlinkat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete

If the command does not return an audit rule for "rename", "unlink", "rmdir", "renameat", and "unlinkat", or any of the lines returned are commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to generate an audit event for any successful/unsuccessful use of the "rename", "unlink", "rmdir", "renameat", "renameat2", and "unlinkat" system calls by adding or updating the following rules in the "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules" file:

-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S rename,unlink,rmdir,renameat,renameat2,unlinkat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S rename,unlink,rmdir,renameat,renameat2,unlinkat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k delete

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without generating audit records that are specific to the security and mission needs of the organization, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

Audit records can be generated from various components within the information system (e.g., module or policy filter).

When a user logs on, the auid is set to the uid of the account that is being authenticated. Daemons are not user sessions and have the loginuid set to -1. The auid representation is an unsigned 32-bit integer, which equals 4294967295. The audit system interprets -1, 4294967295, and "unset" in the same way.

The system call rules are loaded into a matching engine that intercepts each syscall made by all programs on the system. Therefore, it is very important to use syscall rules only when absolutely necessary because these affect performance. More rules lead to poorer performance. The performance can be helped, however, by combining syscalls into one rule whenever possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000037-GPOS-00015, SRG-OS-000042-GPOS-00020, SRG-OS-000062-GPOS-00031, SRG-OS-000392-GPOS-00172, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000471-GPOS-00215, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210, SRG-OS-000467-GPOS-00211, SRG-OS-000468-GPOS-00212

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000130**: Ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 a · Rev 4: AU-3 · Rev 3: AU-3
- **CCI-000135**: Generate audit records containing the organization-defined additional information that is to be included in the audit records.  
  Rev 5: AU-3 (1) · Rev 4: AU-3 (1) · Rev 3: AU-3 (1)
- **CCI-000169**: Provide audit record generation capability for the event types the system is capable of auditing as defined in AU-2 a on organization-defined information system components.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 a · Rev 4: AU-12 a · Rev 3: AU-12 a
- **CCI-002884**: Log organization-defined audit events for nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 4: MA-4 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-281166 · RHEL-10-600000 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must require authentication upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281166r1273588_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must require authentication upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Boot loader (GRUB)*: The small program that starts the operating system when the computer powers on.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, set the GRUB2 superuser password with 'grub2-setpassword' (stored hashed in /boot/grub2/user.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/user.cfg) and set a unique superuser name in /etc/grub.d/01_users. Rescue and emergency modes must require root authentication (sulogin in rescue.service and emergency.service). Mask Ctrl-Alt-Del with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none' in systemd's system.conf. Mask debug-shell. kdump is disabled unless it's needed.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that RHEL 10 requires a password for the GRUB 2 bootloader to prevent unauthorized modifications to boot parameters.

Check the unified configuration file where the GRUB 2 password is stored:

# sudo grep -iw "GRUB2_PASSWORD" /boot/grub2/user.cfg
GRUB2_PASSWORD=grub.pbkdf2.sha512.[password_hash]

If the "GRUB2_PASSWORD" entry does not exist, is commented out, or if the hash does not begin with "grub.pbkdf2.sha512", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to require a grub bootloader password for the grub superuser account.

Generate an encrypted grub2 password for the grub superuser account with the following command:

$ sudo grub2-setpassword
Enter password:
Confirm password:
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To mitigate the risk of unauthorized access to sensitive information by entities that have been issued certificates by DoW-approved PKIs, all DoW systems (e.g., web servers and web portals) must be properly configured to incorporate access control methods that do not rely solely on the possession of a certificate for access.

Successful authentication must not automatically give an entity access to an asset or security boundary. Authorization procedures and controls must be implemented to ensure each authenticated entity also has a validated and current authorization. Authorization is the process of determining whether an entity, once authenticated, is permitted to access a specific asset. Information systems use access control policies and enforcement mechanisms to implement this requirement.

Password protection on the boot loader configuration ensures users with physical access cannot trivially alter important bootloader settings. These include which kernel to use and whether to enter single-user mode.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

---

### V-281167 · RHEL-10-600010 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must require a unique superusers name upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must require a unique superusers name upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Boot loader (GRUB)*: The small program that starts the operating system when the computer powers on.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/grub.d/01_users | export | superusers |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set the GRUB2 superuser password with 'grub2-setpassword' (stored hashed in /boot/grub2/user.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/user.cfg) and set a unique superuser name in /etc/grub.d/01_users. Rescue and emergency modes must require root authentication (sulogin in rescue.service and emergency.service). Mask Ctrl-Alt-Del with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none' in systemd's system.conf. Mask debug-shell. kdump is disabled unless it's needed.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 requires a unique superusers name upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

Verify that the boot loader superuser account has been set with the following command:

$ sudo grep -A1 "superusers" /etc/grub2.cfg
set superusers="<accountname>"
export superusers
password_pbkdf2 <accountname> ${GRUB2_PASSWORD}

Verify <accountname> is not a common name such as root, admin, or administrator.

If superusers contains easily guessable usernames, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have a unique username for the grub superuser account.

Edit the "/etc/grub.d/01_users" file and add or modify the following lines with a nondefault username for the superuser account:

set superusers="<accountname>"
export superusers

Once the superuser account has been added, update the "grub.cfg" file by regenerating the GRUB configuration with the following command:

$ sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg --update-bls-cmdline

Reboot the system:

$ sudo reboot
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Having a nondefault grub superuser username makes password-guessing attacks less effective.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.
