### V-281168 · RHEL-10-600020 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must not assign an interactive login shell for system accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281168r1273589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000445-GPOS-00199 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-002696 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not assign an interactive login shell for system accounts.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that RHEL 10 system accounts do not have an interactive login shell.

Run the following command to list any system account (UID < 1000) that has an interactive shell, excluding authorized system utility accounts (root, sync, shutdown, halt):

$ $ awk -F: '(($3 > 0 && $3 < 1000) && $1 !~ /^(halt|sync|shutdown)$/ && $7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/) {print $1 ":" $3 ":" $7}' /etc/passwd

If the command returns any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that all noninteractive accounts on the system do not have an interactive shell assigned to them.

If the system account needs a shell assigned for mission operations, document the need with the information system security officer (ISSO).

Run the following command to disable the interactive shell for a specific noninteractive user account:

$ sudo usermod --shell /usr/sbin/nologin <user>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Ensuring shells are not given to system accounts upon login makes it more difficult for attackers to use system accounts.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002696**: Verify correct operation of organization-defined security functions.  
  Rev 5: SI-6 a · Rev 4: SI-6 a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281169 · RHEL-10-600100 · CAT II: RHEL 10 user account passwords for new users or password changes must have a 180-day maximum password lifetime restriction in /etc/login.defs.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281169r1273590_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000076-GPOS-00044 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse, Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's user account passwords for new users or password changes must have a 180-day maximum password lifetime restriction in /etc/login.defs.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | PASS_MAX_DAYS | 180 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Also related (Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory)):** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that RHEL 10 enforces a 180-day maximum password lifetime for new user accounts by running the following command:

$ sudo grep -i pass_max_days /etc/login.defs
PASS_MAX_DAYS 180

If the "PASS_MAX_DAYS" parameter value is greater than "180", or commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce a 180-day maximum password lifetime.

Add, or modify the following line in the "/etc/login.defs" file:

PASS_MAX_DAYS 180
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Any password, no matter how complex, can eventually be cracked; therefore, passwords need to be changed periodically. If the operating system does not limit the lifetime of passwords and force users to change their passwords, there is the risk that the operating system passwords could be compromised.

Setting the password maximum age ensures users are required to periodically change their passwords. Requiring shorter password lifetimes increases the risk of users writing down the password in a convenient location subject to physical compromise.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing; T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281171 · RHEL-10-600120 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must assign a home directory for local interactive user accounts upon creation.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281171r1166465_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000433-GPOS-00192 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-002824 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-16 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-16 |

### V-281173 · RHEL-10-600140 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281173r1166471_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000123-GPOS-00064 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-001682, CCI-000016 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 automatically expires temporary accounts within 72 hours.

For every existing temporary account, run the following command to obtain its account expiration information:

$ sudo chage -l <temporary_account_name> | grep -i "account expires"

Verify each of these accounts has an expiration date set within 72 hours.

If any temporary accounts have no expiration date set or do not expire within 72 hours, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to expire temporary accounts after 72 hours with the following command:

$ sudo chage -E $(date -d +3days +%Y-%m-%d) <temporary_account_name>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Temporary accounts are privileged or nonprivileged accounts that are established during pressing circumstances, such as new software or hardware configuration or an incident response, where the need for prompt account activation requires bypassing normal account authorization procedures. If any inactive temporary accounts are left enabled on the system and are not manually removed or automatically expired within 72 hours, the security posture of the system will be degraded and exposed to exploitation by unauthorized users or insider threat actors.

Temporary accounts are different from emergency accounts. Emergency accounts, also known as "last resort" or "break glass" accounts, are local login accounts enabled on the system for emergency use by authorized system administrators to manage a system when standard login methods are failing or not available. Emergency accounts are not subject to manual removal or scheduled expiration requirements.

The automatic expiration of temporary accounts may be extended as needed by the circumstances, but it must not be extended indefinitely. A documented permanent account should be established for privileged users who need long-term maintenance accounts.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000123-GPOS-00064, SRG-OS-000002-GPOS-00002

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001682**: Automatically remove or disable emergency accounts after an organization-defined time period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)
- **CCI-000016**: Automatically remove or disable temporary and emergency accounts after an organization-defined time-period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)

#### Level 3: General Audience

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 local interactive user initialization file executable search path statements do not contain statements that will reference a working directory other than user home directories with the following commands:

$ sudo find /home -maxdepth 2 -type f -name ".[^.]*" -exec grep -iH path= {} \;
PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$HOME/bin:$PATH"

If any local interactive user initialization files have executable search path statements that include directories outside of their home directory, and this is not documented with the ISSO as an operational requirement, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that all local interactive user initialization file executable search path statements do not contain statements that will reference a working directory other than user home directories.

Edit the local interactive user initialization files to change any PATH variable statements that reference directories other than their home directory.

If a local interactive user requires path variables to reference a directory owned by the application, it must be documented with the ISSO.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The executable search path (typically the PATH environment variable) contains a list of directories for the shell to search to find executables. If this path includes the current working directory (other than the user's home directory), executables in these directories may be executed instead of system commands.

This variable is formatted as a colon-separated list of directories. If there is an empty entry, such as a leading or trailing colon or two consecutive colons, this is interpreted as the current working directory. If deviations from the default system search path for the local interactive user are required, they must be documented with the information system security officer (ISSO).

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 interactive users' home directories to exist on the system.

Create home directories to all local interactive users that do not have a home directory assigned. Use the following commands to create the user home directory assigned in "/etc/ passwd":

Note: The example will be for the user "disauser", who has a home directory of "/home/disauser", a user identifier (UID) of "disauser", and a group identifier (GID) of "users assigned" in "/etc/passwd".

$ sudo mkdir /home/disauser
$ sudo chown disauser /home/disauser
$ sudo chgrp users /home/disauser
$ sudo chmod 0750 /home/disauser
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If a local interactive user has a home directory defined that does not exist, the user may be given access to the / directory as the current working directory upon login. This could create a denial of service because the user would not be able to access their login configuration files, and it may give them visibility to system files they normally would not be able to access.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281179 · RHEL-10-600200 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enforce a delay of at least four seconds between login prompts following a failed login attempt.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281179r1166489_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128 |
| Topic | Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-002238 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce a delay of at least four seconds between login prompts following a failed login attempt.

**Why it matters:** Behind the sign-in screen is a chain of checks: the password is right, the account isn't locked, the password isn't expired, and so on. This rule makes sure every check in that chain is present and in the correct order, like making sure every guard at a multi-checkpoint entrance is at their post.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | FAIL_DELAY | 4 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** PAM mistakes can lock everyone out, including root. Test changes from a second, still-open root session, and keep console access available.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces a delay of at least four seconds between console login prompts following a failed login attempt with the following command:

$ sudo grep -i fail_delay /etc/login.defs
FAIL_DELAY 4

If the value of "FAIL_DELAY" is not set to "4" or greater, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce a delay of at least four seconds between login prompts following a failed console login attempt.

Modify the "/etc/login.defs" file to set the "FAIL_DELAY" parameter to "4" or greater:

FAIL_DELAY 4
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Increasing the time between a failed authentication attempt and reprompting to enter credentials helps to slow a single-threaded brute-force attack.

**Threat & control context:** PAM and SSSD define how every Linux authentication decision is made. Misordered or optional modules silently bypass controls such as faillock, pwquality and pwhistory. Credential caching lifetimes trade availability against revocation latency, so a revoked account keeps working offline until its cache expires. These settings support IA-2, IA-5(13) (expiration of cached authenticators), AC-7, AC-9 (previous logon notification) and AC-10 (concurrent session control).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281180 · RHEL-10-600210 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enforce a 24-hours minimum password lifetime restriction for passwords for new users or password changes in "/etc/login.defs".

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281180r1166492_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000075-GPOS-00043 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse, Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce a 24-hours minimum password lifetime restriction for passwords for new users or password changes in "/etc/login.defs".

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | PASS_MIN_DAYS | 1 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Also related (Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory)):** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces 24 hours as the minimum password lifetime for new user accounts.

Check for the value of "PASS_MIN_DAYS" in "/etc/login.defs" with the following command:

$ sudo grep -i pass_min_days /etc/login.defs
PASS_MIN_DAYS 1

If the "PASS_MIN_DAYS" parameter value is not "1" or greater or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce 24 hours as the minimum password lifetime.

Add the following line in "/etc/login.defs" (or modify the line to have the required value):

PASS_MIN_DAYS 1
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enforcing a minimum password lifetime helps to prevent repeated password changes to defeat the password reuse or history enforcement requirement. If users are allowed to immediately and continually change their password, the password could be repeatedly changed in a short period of time to defeat the organization's policy regarding password reuse.

Setting the minimum password age protects against users cycling back to a favorite password after satisfying the password reuse requirement.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing; T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281181 · RHEL-10-600220 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enforce that passwords be created with a minimum of 15 characters.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281181r1273592_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000078-GPOS-00046 |
| Topic | Password Strength & Complexity |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce that passwords be created with a minimum of 15 characters.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d | minlen | 15 |

**How it works:** RHEL enforces this through pam_pwquality, configured in /etc/security/pwquality.conf or a drop-in under /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/ (minlen, dcredit/ucredit/lcredit/ocredit as negative numbers meaning 'at least N', minclass, maxrepeat, maxclassrepeat, difok, dictcheck). The pam_pwquality module must appear in the password stack of system-auth and password-auth. Test with 'pwscore' or by changing a test user's password.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces a minimum 15-character password length with the following command:

$ sudo grep -s minlen /etc/security/pwquality.conf /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/*.conf
/etc/security/pwquality.conf:minlen = 15

If the command does not return a "minlen" value of "15" or greater, does not return a line, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce a minimum 15-character password length.

Add or update the following line in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf" file or a configuration file in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/" directory to contain the "minlen" parameter:

minlen = 15
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The shorter the password, the lower the number of possible combinations that must be tested before the password is compromised.

Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute-force attacks. Password length is one factor of several that helps to determine strength and how long it takes to crack a password. Use of more characters in a password helps to increase exponentially the time and/or resources required to compromise the password.

RHEL 10 uses "pwquality" as a mechanism to enforce password complexity. Configurations are set in the "etc/security/pwquality.conf" file.

The "minlen", sometimes noted as minimum length, acts as a "score" of complexity based on the credit components of the "pwquality" module. By setting the credit components to a negative value, those components will not only be required but will not count toward the total "score" of "minlen". This will enable "minlen" to require a 15-character minimum.

The DoW minimum password requirement is 15 characters.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

**How it works:** RHEL enforces this through pam_pwquality, configured in /etc/security/pwquality.conf or a drop-in under /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/ (minlen, dcredit/ucredit/lcredit/ocredit as negative numbers meaning 'at least N', minclass, maxrepeat, maxclassrepeat, difok, dictcheck). The pam_pwquality module must appear in the password stack of system-auth and password-auth. Test with 'pwscore' or by changing a test user's password.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 requires the change of at least eight characters when passwords are changed by checking the value of the "difok" option in "/etc/security/pwquality.conf" with the following command:

$ sudo grep difok -s /etc/security/pwquality.conf /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/*.conf
/etc/security/pwquality.conf:difok = 8

If the value of "difok" is set to less than "8" or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to require the change of at least eight of the total number of characters when passwords are changed by setting the "difok" option.

Add or update the following line in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf" file or a configuration file in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/" directory to contain the "difok" parameter:

difok = 8
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of a complex password helps to increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute–force attacks.

Password complexity is one factor of several that determines how long it takes to crack a password. The more complex the password, the greater the number of possible combinations that must be tested before the password is compromised.

Requiring a minimum number of different characters during password changes ensures that newly changed passwords should not resemble previously compromised ones.

Note that passwords that are changed on compromised systems will still be compromised.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281186 · RHEL-10-600270 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enforce that passwords have a 24 hours/1 day minimum lifetime restriction in "/etc/shadow".

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281186r1184622_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000075-GPOS-00043 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce that passwords have a 24 hours/1 day minimum lifetime restriction in "/etc/shadow".

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the minimum time period between password changes for each user account is one day or greater with the following command:

$ sudo awk -F: '$4 < 1 {printf "%s %d\n", $1, $4}' /etc/shadow

If any results are returned that are not associated with a system account, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that noncompliant accounts enforce a 24 hours/1 day minimum password lifetime:

$ sudo passwd -n 1 [user]
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enforcing a minimum password lifetime helps to prevent repeated password changes to defeat the password reuse or history enforcement requirement. If users are allowed to immediately and continually change their password, the password could be repeatedly changed in a short period of time to defeat the organization's policy for password reuse.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281192 · RHEL-10-600400 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must allow only the root account to have unrestricted access to the system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281192r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must allow only the root account to have unrestricted access to the system.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that only the "root" account has a UID "0" assignment with the following command:

$ awk -F: '$3 == 0 {print $1}' /etc/passwd
root

If any accounts other than "root" have a UID of "0", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that only the "root" account has a UID assignment of "0".

Change the UID of any account on the system, other than "root", that has a UID of "0".

If the account is associated with system commands or applications, the UID should be changed to one greater than "0" but less than "1000". Otherwise, assign a UID of greater than "1000" that has not already been assigned.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** An account has root authority if it has a user identifier (UID) of "0". Multiple accounts with a UID of "0" afford more opportunity for potential intruders to guess a password for a privileged account. Proper configuration of sudo is recommended to afford multiple system administrators access to root privileges in an accountable manner.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281193 · RHEL-10-600405 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enforce password complexity rules for the "root" account.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281193r1166531_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000072-GPOS-00040 |
| Topic | Password Strength & Complexity |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce password complexity rules for the "root" account.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** RHEL enforces this through pam_pwquality, configured in /etc/security/pwquality.conf or a drop-in under /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/ (minlen, dcredit/ucredit/lcredit/ocredit as negative numbers meaning 'at least N', minclass, maxrepeat, maxclassrepeat, difok, dictcheck). The pam_pwquality module must appear in the password stack of system-auth and password-auth. Test with 'pwscore' or by changing a test user's password.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces password complexity rules for the "root" account.

Check if "root" user is required to use complex passwords with the following command:

$ sudo grep enforce_for_root /etc/security/pwquality.conf /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/*.conf
/etc/security/pwquality.conf:enforce_for_root

If "enforce_for_root" is commented out or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce password complexity on the "root" account.

Add or update the following line in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf" file or a configuration file in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/" directory to contain the "enforce_for_root" parameter:

enforce_for_root
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of a complex password helps to increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute-force attacks.

Password complexity is one factor of several that determines how long it takes to crack a password. The more complex the password, the greater the number of possible combinations that must be tested before the password is compromised.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000072-GPOS-00040, SRG-OS-000071-GPOS-00039, SRG-OS-000070-GPOS-00038, SRG-OS-000266-GPOS-00101, SRG-OS-000078-GPOS-00046, SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00225, SRG-OS-000069-GPOS-00037

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281194 · RHEL-10-600410 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must automatically lock an account when three unsuccessful login attempts occur.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281194r1166534_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-002238, CCI-000044 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 b, AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 b, AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically lock an account when three unsuccessful login attempts occur.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/security/faillock.conf | deny | 3 |

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Also related (Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout):** On RHEL, set GNOME locking through dconf in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/ (org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900, org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, lock-delay=uint32 5) and lock each key in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/ so users can't override it. Then run 'dconf update'. For terminals, set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. Network and SSH sessions use ClientAliveInterval/CountMax and systemd-logind StopIdleSessionSec.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to lock an account after three unsuccessful login attempts with the following command:

$ sudo grep 'deny =' /etc/security/faillock.conf
deny = 3

If the "deny" option is not set to "3" or less (but not "0"), or is missing or commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to lock an account when three unsuccessful login attempts occur.

Add/modify the "/etc/security/faillock.conf" file to match the following line:

deny = 3
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** By limiting the number of failed login attempts, the risk of unauthorized system access via user password guessing, otherwise known as brute-force attacks, is reduced. Limits are imposed by locking the account.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128, SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a


#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Having lockouts persist across reboots ensures that an account is unlocked only by an administrator. If the lockouts did not persist across reboots, an attacker could reboot the system to continue brute force attacks against the accounts on the system.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005, SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a
- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281199 · RHEL-10-600450 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must not have unauthorized accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281199r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not have unauthorized accounts.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 has no unauthorized local interactive user accounts with the following command:

$ less /etc/passwd
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
...
nsauser:x:1000:1000:nsauser:/home/nsauser:/bin/bash
doduser:x:1001:1001:doduser:/home/doduser:/bin/bash

Interactive user accounts generally will have a user ID (UID) of 1000 or greater, a home directory in a specific partition, and an interactive shell.

Obtain the list of interactive user accounts authorized to be on the system from the system administrator or information system security officer and compare it to the list of local interactive user accounts on the system.

If there are unauthorized local user accounts on the system, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have no unauthorized local interactive user accounts with the following command, where <unauthorized_user> is the unauthorized account:

$ sudo userdel  <unauthorized_user>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Having lockouts persist across reboots ensures that account is unlocked only by an administrator. If the lockouts did not persist across reboots, an attacker could reboot the system to continue brute force attacks against the accounts on the system.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281200 · RHEL-10-600455 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must not allow blank or null passwords.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281200r1166552_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000069-GPOS-00037 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not allow blank or null passwords.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 prohibits the use of null passwords with the following command:

$ sudo grep -i nullok /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth

If output is produced, this is a finding.

If the system administrator (SA) can demonstrate that the required configuration is contained in a PAM configuration file included or substacked from the "system-auth" file, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prohibit the use of null passwords.

If PAM is managed with "authselect", use the following command to remove instances of "nullok":

$ sudo authselect enable-feature without-nullok

Otherwise, remove any instances of the "nullok" option in the "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" and "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" files to prevent logins with empty passwords.

Note: Manual changes to the listed file may be overwritten by the "authselect" program.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If an account has an empty password, anyone could log in and run commands with the privileges of that account. Accounts with empty passwords must never be used in operational environments.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

---

| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have a unique group ID (GID) for each group in "/etc/group".

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 contains no duplicate GIDs for interactive users with the following command:

 $  cut -d : -f 3 /etc/group | uniq -d
```

```text
Edit the file "/etc/group", and provide each group that has a duplicate GID with a unique GID.
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To ensure accountability and prevent unauthenticated access, groups must be identified uniquely to prevent potential misuse and compromise of the system.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. ### V-281203 · RHEL-10-600475 · CAT III: RHEL 10 must limit the number of concurrent sessions to 10 for all accounts and/or account types.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281203r1166561_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000027-GPOS-00008 |
| Topic | Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-000054 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-10 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-10 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-10 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must limit the number of concurrent sessions to 10 for all accounts and/or account types.

**Why it matters:** Behind the sign-in screen is a chain of checks: the password is right, the account isn't locked, the password isn't expired, and so on. This rule makes sure every check in that chain is present and in the correct order, like making sure every guard at a multi-checkpoint entrance is at their post.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** PAM mistakes can lock everyone out, including root. Test changes from a second, still-open root session, and keep console access available.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 limits the number of concurrent sessions to "10" for all accounts and/or account types with the following command:

$ sudo grep -rs maxlogins /etc/security/limits.conf /etc/security/limits.d/*.conf | grep -v '#'
/etc/security/limits.d/maxlogins.conf:* hard maxlogins 10

This can be set as a global domain (with the * wildcard) but may be set differently for multiple domains.

If the "maxlogins" item is missing or commented out, or the value is set greater than "10" and is not documented with the information system security officer as an operational requirement for all domains that have the "maxlogins" item assigned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to limit the number of concurrent sessions to "10" for all accounts and/or account types.

Add the following line to the top of "/etc/security/limits.conf" or in a ".conf" file defined in "/etc/security/limits.d/":

* hard maxlogins 10
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Operating system management includes the ability to control the number of users and user sessions that use an operating system. Limiting the number of allowed users and sessions per user is helpful in reducing the risks related to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.

This requirement addresses concurrent sessions for information system accounts and does not address concurrent sessions by single users via multiple system accounts. The maximum number of concurrent sessions should be defined based on mission needs and the operational environment for each system.

**Threat & control context:** PAM and SSSD define how every Linux authentication decision is made. Misordered or optional modules silently bypass controls such as faillock, pwquality and pwhistory. Credential caching lifetimes trade availability against revocation latency, so a revoked account keeps working offline until its cache expires. These settings support IA-2, IA-5(13) (expiration of cached authenticators), AC-7, AC-9 (previous logon notification) and AC-10 (concurrent session control).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000054**: Limit the number of concurrent sessions for each organization-defined account and/or account type to an organization-defined number.  
  Rev 5: AC-10 · Rev 4: AC-10 · Rev 3: AC-10

### V-281204 · RHEL-10-600485 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must ensure the password complexity module in the system-auth file is configured for three or fewer retries.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281204r1197240_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000069-GPOS-00037 |
| Topic | Password Strength & Complexity |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must ensure the password complexity module in the system-auth file is configured for three or fewer retries.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d | retry | 3 |

**How it works:** RHEL enforces this through pam_pwquality, configured in /etc/security/pwquality.conf or a drop-in under /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/ (minlen, dcredit/ucredit/lcredit/ocredit as negative numbers meaning 'at least N', minclass, maxrepeat, maxclassrepeat, difok, dictcheck). The pam_pwquality module must appear in the password stack of system-auth and password-auth. Test with 'pwscore' or by changing a test user's password.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to limit the "pwquality" retry option to "3" with the following command:

$ sudo grep -w retry /etc/security/pwquality.conf /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/*.conf
retry = 3

If the value of "retry" is set to "0" or greater than "3", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to limit the "pwquality" retry option to "3".

Add or update the following line in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf" file or a file in the "/etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/" directory to contain the "retry" parameter:

retry = 3
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of a complex password helps to increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute-force attacks. "pwquality" enforces complex password construction configuration and has the ability to limit brute-force attacks on the system.

RHEL 10 uses "pwquality" as a mechanism to enforce password complexity. This is set in both of the following:

"/etc/pam.d/password-auth"
"/etc/pam.d/system-auth"

By limiting the number of attempts to meet the pwquality module complexity requirements before returning with an error, the system will audit abnormal attempts at password changes.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

---

### V-281205 · RHEL-10-600500 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must restrict the use of the "su" command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281205r1166567_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000373-GPOS-00156 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo) |
| CCI | CCI-002038, CCI-002165 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-11, AC-3 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-11, AC-3 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must restrict the use of the "su" command.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/su | auth | required    pam_wheel.so use_uid |

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 requires users to be members of the "wheel" group to run "su".

Verify the configuration with the following command:

$ sudo grep pam_wheel /etc/pam.d/su
auth             required        pam_wheel.so use_uid

If a line for "pam_wheel.so" does not exist or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to require users to be in the "wheel" group to run the "su" command.

Edit the configuration file:

$ sudo vi /etc/pam.d/su

Add the following lines:

auth    required    pam_wheel.so use_uid
$ sed '/^[[:space:]]*#[[:space:]]*auth[[:space:]]\+required[[:space:]]\+pam_wheel\.so[[:space:]]\+use_uid$/s/^[[:space:]]*#//' -i /etc/pam.d/su

If necessary, create a "wheel" group and add administrative users to the group.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "su" program allows commands to be run with a substitute user and group ID. It is commonly used to run commands as the root user. Limiting access to such commands is considered a good security practice.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000373-GPOS-00156, SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00123

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
