### V-281212 · RHEL-10-600600 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must configure the use of the pam_faillock.so module in the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" file.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281212r1166588_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-000044 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must configure the use of the pam_faillock.so module in the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" file.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/system-auth | auth | required pam_faillock.so preauth |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/system-auth | auth | required pam_faillock.so authfail |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/system-auth | account | required pam_faillock.so |

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Also related (Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory)):** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 includes the use of the pam_faillock.so module in the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" file:

$ sudo grep pam_faillock.so /etc/pam.d/system-auth
auth required pam_faillock.so preauth
auth required pam_faillock.so authfail
account required pam_faillock.so

If the pam_faillock.so module is not present in the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" file with the "preauth" line listed before pam_unix.so, this is a finding.

If the system administrator can demonstrate that the required configuration is contained in a PAM configuration file included or substacked from the "system-auth" file, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to include the use of the pam_faillock.so module in the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" file.

If PAM is managed with authselect, enable the feature with the following command:

$ sudo authselect enable-feature with-faillock

Otherwise, add/modify the appropriate sections of the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" file to match the following lines:

Note: The "preauth" line must be listed before pam_unix.so.

auth required pam_faillock.so preauth
auth required pam_faillock.so authfail
account required pam_faillock.so
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If the pam_faillock.so module is not loaded, the system will not correctly lock out accounts to prevent password guessing attacks.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a

### V-281213 · RHEL-10-600610 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must configure the use of the pam_faillock.so module in the "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" file.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281213r1166591_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-000044 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must configure the use of the pam_faillock.so module in the "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" file.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | auth | required pam_faillock.so preauth |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | auth | required pam_faillock.so authfail |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | account | required pam_faillock.so |

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Also related (Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory)):** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

auth required pam_faillock.so preauth
auth required pam_faillock.so authfail
account required pam_faillock.so

If the pam_faillock.so module is not present in the "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" file with the "preauth" line listed before pam_unix.so, this is a finding.

If the system administrator can demonstrate that the required configuration is contained in a Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) configuration file included or substacked from the "system-auth" file, this is not a finding.
```

$ sudo authselect enable-feature with-faillock

Otherwise, add/modify the appropriate sections of the "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" file to match the following lines:

Note: The "preauth" line must be listed before pam_unix.so.

auth required pam_faillock.so preauth
auth required pam_faillock.so authfail
account required pam_faillock.so
```

The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

### V-281214 · RHEL-10-600620 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must ensure the password complexity module is enabled in the "password-auth" file.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281214r1166594_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000069-GPOS-00037 |
| Topic | Password Strength & Complexity |
| CCI | CCI-004066 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must ensure the password complexity module is enabled in the "password-auth" file.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | password | required pam_pwquality.so |

**How it works:** RHEL enforces this through pam_pwquality, configured in /etc/security/pwquality.conf or a drop-in under /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/ (minlen, dcredit/ucredit/lcredit/ocredit as negative numbers meaning 'at least N', minclass, maxrepeat, maxclassrepeat, difok, dictcheck). The pam_pwquality module must appear in the password stack of system-auth and password-auth. Test with 'pwscore' or by changing a test user's password.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 uses "pwquality" to enforce the password complexity rules in the "password-auth" file with the following command:

$ sudo grep pam_pwquality /etc/pam.d/password-auth
password required pam_pwquality.so

If the command does not return a line containing the value "pam_pwquality.so", or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

If the system administrator can demonstrate that the required configuration is contained in a PAM configuration file included or substacked from the "system-auth" file, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use "pwquality" to enforce password complexity rules.

Add the following line to the "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" file (or modify the line to have the required value):

password required pam_pwquality.so
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enabling Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) password complexity permits enforcement of strong passwords and consequently makes the system less prone to dictionary attacks.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000069-GPOS-00037, SRG-OS-000070-GPOS-00038

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281216 · RHEL-10-600640 · CAT I: RHEL 10 must enable the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface for SSHD.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281216r1166600_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000125-GPOS-00065 |
| Topic | SSH Remote Administration, Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-000877 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | MA-4 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | MA-4 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | MA-4 c |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enable the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface for SSHD.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d | UsePAM | yes |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory)):** On RHEL, PAM stacks live in /etc/pam.d/ (system-auth, password-auth, login, sshd, su). Manage them through authselect profiles ('authselect select sssd with-faillock with-mkhomedir ...', 'authselect current'), because authselect overwrites hand edits. Custom changes belong in a custom profile ('authselect create-profile'). SSSD is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf and conf.d/ (mode 0600, owned by root), and you restart sssd after changes. Concurrent session limits are set in /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard maxlogins 10').

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 SSHD is configured to allow for the "UsePAM" interface with the following command:

$ sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -dd 2>&1 | awk '/filename/ {print $4}' | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' ' | xargs sudo grep -iH '^\s*usepam'
UsePAM yes

If the "UsePAM" keyword is set to "no", is missing, or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 SSHD to use the "UsePAM" interface by adding or modifying the following line in "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" or in a file in "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d".

UsePAM yes

Restart the SSH daemon with the following command for the settings to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When "UsePAM" is set to "yes", PAM runs through account and session types properly. This is important when restricted access to services based on IP, time, or other factors of the account is needed. Additionally, this ensures users can inherit certain environment variables on login or disallow access to the server.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000877**: Employ strong authentication in the establishment of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 c · Rev 4: MA-4 c · Rev 3: MA-4 c

### V-281217 · RHEL-10-600650 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must ensure that the pam_unix.so module is configured in the password-auth file to use a FIPS 140-3-approved cryptographic hashing algorithm for system authentication.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281217r1273593_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140), Credential Storage & Password Hashing |
| CCI | CCI-004062, CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (d), IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must ensure that the pam_unix.so module is configured in the password-auth file to use a FIPS 140-3-approved cryptographic hashing algorithm for system authentication.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/password-auth | password | sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 |

**How it works:** RHEL centralizes crypto settings in system-wide crypto policies: 'fips-mode-setup --enable' (RHEL 8) or 'fips=1' on the kernel command line at install time (RHEL 9/10), then 'update-crypto-policies --set FIPS'. Back-end files under /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ (openssh, opensslcnf, bind, gnutls and others) are generated from the policy, and individual services such as sshd must be pointed at them rather than hard-coding algorithms. Verify with 'fips-mode-setup --check' and 'update-crypto-policies --show'.

**Also related (Credential Storage & Password Hashing):** On RHEL, hashes are stored in /etc/shadow. The algorithm for new passwords comes from ENCRYPT_METHOD (and SHA_CRYPT_MIN_ROUNDS) in /etc/login.defs, 'crypt_style' in /etc/libuser.conf, and the pam_unix module options. Existing hashes are upgraded only when users change their passwords. Check the hash prefix in /etc/shadow ($6$ = SHA-512).

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 configures the pam_unix.so module to use sha512 in "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" with the following command:

$ sudo grep "^password.*pam_unix.so.*sha512" /etc/pam.d/password-auth
password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512

If "sha512" is missing, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use the sha512 cryptographic hashing algorithm for local account passwords.

Edit/modify the following line in the "/etc/pam.d/password-auth" file to include the sha512 option for pam_unix.so:

password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unapproved mechanisms that are used for authentication to the cryptographic module are not verified; therefore, they cannot be relied on to provide confidentiality or integrity, and DoW data may be compromised.

RHEL 10 systems using encryption are required to use FIPS-compliant mechanisms for authenticating to cryptographic modules.

FIPS 140-3 is the current standard for validating that mechanisms used to access cryptographic modules use authentication that meets DoW requirements. This allows for Security Levels 1, 2, 3, or 4 for use on a general-purpose computing system.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041, SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004062**: For password-based authentication, store passwords using an approved salted key derivation function, preferably using a keyed hash.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000803**: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for such authentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-7 · Rev 4: IA-7 · Rev 3: IA-7

### V-281218 · RHEL-10-600700 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured to use a sufficient number of hashing rounds for the shadow password suite.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281218r1166606_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing |
| CCI | CCI-004062, CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (d), IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to use a sufficient number of hashing rounds for the shadow password suite.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/system-auth | password | sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 rounds=100000 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, hashes are stored in /etc/shadow. The algorithm for new passwords comes from ENCRYPT_METHOD (and SHA_CRYPT_MIN_ROUNDS) in /etc/login.defs, 'crypt_style' in /etc/libuser.conf, and the pam_unix module options. Existing hashes are upgraded only when users change their passwords. Check the hash prefix in /etc/shadow ($6$ = SHA-512).

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 uses a sufficient number of rounds for the shadow password suite hashing algorithm with the following command:

$ sudo grep rounds /etc/pam.d/system-auth
password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 rounds=100000

If the setting is not configured or "rounds" is less than 100000, this a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use a sufficient number of hashing rounds for shadow password suite.

Add or modify the following line in "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" and set "rounds" to 100000:

password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 rounds=100000
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Passwords must be protected at all times, and encryption is the standard method for protecting passwords. If passwords are not encrypted, they can be plainly read (i.e., clear text) and easily compromised. Passwords that are encrypted with a weak algorithm are no more protected than if they are kept in plain text.

Using more hashing rounds makes password cracking attacks more difficult.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041, SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004062**: For password-based authentication, store passwords using an approved salted key derivation function, preferably using a keyed hash.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000803**: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for such authentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-7 · Rev 4: IA-7 · Rev 3: IA-7

### V-281219 · RHEL-10-600710 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured to use a FIPS 140-3-approved cryptographic hashing algorithm for system authentication by ensuring that the pam_unix.so module is configured in the "system-auth" file.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281219r1273594_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140), Software & File Integrity Verification |
| CCI | CCI-004062, CCI-000803 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (d), IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-7 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-7 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to use a FIPS 140-3-approved cryptographic hashing algorithm for system authentication by ensuring that the pam_unix.so module is configured in the "system-auth" file.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/system-auth | password | sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 |

**How it works:** RHEL centralizes crypto settings in system-wide crypto policies: 'fips-mode-setup --enable' (RHEL 8) or 'fips=1' on the kernel command line at install time (RHEL 9/10), then 'update-crypto-policies --set FIPS'. Back-end files under /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/ (openssh, opensslcnf, bind, gnutls and others) are generated from the policy, and individual services such as sshd must be pointed at them rather than hard-coding algorithms. Verify with 'fips-mode-setup --check' and 'update-crypto-policies --show'.

**Also related (Software & File Integrity Verification):** On RHEL, repositories must have 'gpgcheck=1' (/etc/dnf/dnf.conf and /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo) and 'localpkg_gpgcheck=1', with Red Hat GPG keys imported ('rpm -q gpg-pubkey'). AIDE is configured in /etc/aide.conf (rules should include acl, xattrs and sha512). Initialize with 'aide --init' and move the new database into place. Schedule 'aide --check' daily (cron or systemd timer) with notification to the SA/ISSO.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java and .NET code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). Enable it at install time where possible, because switching an existing RHEL 9/10 system into FIPS mode is not supported for production. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to use a FIPS 140-3-approved cryptographic hashing algorithm in "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" via the pam_unix.so module with the following command:

$ sudo grep "^password.*pam_unix.so.*sha512" /etc/pam.d/system-auth
password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512

If "sha512" is missing, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use a FIPS 140-3-approved cryptographic hashing algorithm for system authentication in "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" via the "pam_unix.so" module.

Edit/modify the following line in the "/etc/pam.d/system-auth" file to include the sha512 option for pam_unix.so:

password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unapproved mechanisms that are used for authentication to the cryptographic module are not verified and therefore cannot be relied on to provide confidentiality or integrity, and DoW data may be compromised.

RHEL 10 systems using encryption are required to use FIPS-compliant mechanisms for authenticating to cryptographic modules.

FIPS 140-3 is the current standard for validating that mechanisms used to access cryptographic modules use authentication that meets DoW requirements. This allows for Security Levels 1, 2, 3, or 4 for use on a general-purpose computing system.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041, SRG-OS-000120-GPOS-00061

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption; T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary; T1014 Rootkit

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004062**: For password-based authentication, store passwords using an approved salted key derivation function, preferably using a keyed hash.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000803**: Implement mechanisms for authentication to a cryptographic module that meet the requirements of applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance for such authentication.  
  Rev 5: IA-7 · Rev 4: IA-7 · Rev 3: IA-7

**In plain terms:** This computer must display the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner before granting local or remote access to the system via a Secure Shell (SSH) login.

**Why it matters:** Before anyone can sign in, the computer shows a warning message saying the system belongs to the government, that activity is monitored, and that using it means you agree to that. Think of it like the "this area is under video surveillance" sign at the entrance to a building: it doesn't lock the door, but it makes the rules clear and discourages misuse.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d | Banner | /etc/issue |

**How it works:** On RHEL the banner is typically set in /etc/issue (console and SSH pre-auth via the sshd 'Banner' directive) and in the GNOME login screen via dconf ('banner-message-enable' and 'banner-message-text'). The text must match the DoD standard banner exactly, including line breaks where the check text calls for them.

**Also related (SSH Remote Administration):** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Operational impact:** No functional impact. Automated logons and kiosk workflows will need to acknowledge the banner, and some scanners compare the text byte-for-byte, so copy it from the STIG rather than retyping it.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that any SSH connection to the operating system displays the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner before granting access to the system.

Check for the location of the banner file currently being used with the following command:

$ sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -dd 2>&1 | awk '/filename/ {print $4}' | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' ' | xargs sudo grep -iH '^\s*banner'
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-stig.conf:Banner /etc/issue

If the line is commented out or the file is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to display the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner before granting access to the system via SSH.

Edit a file in "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d" to uncomment or add the banner keyword and configure it to point to a file that will contain the login banner (this file may be named differently or be in a different location if using a version of SSH that is provided by a third-party vendor).

An example configuration line is:

Banner /etc/issue
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The warning message reinforces policy awareness during the login process and facilitates possible legal action against attackers. Alternatively, systems whose ownership should not be obvious should ensure use of a banner that does not provide easy attribution.

OpenSSH uses the first occurrence of a keyword it sees, and drop-in files are read in lexicographical order at the start of the configuration. Red Hat recommends using drop-in files rather than changing base configuration files.

**Threat & control context:** A notice-and-consent banner is a legal and deterrence control rather than a technical barrier. It establishes that users have no expectation of privacy, which supports monitoring, incident response and prosecution, and it satisfies AC-8 (System Use Notification). Assessors verify the exact approved DoD text, that it appears for every access path (console, GUI, SSH and other remote sessions), and that the user must acknowledge it before the session continues.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281225 · RHEL-10-700020 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must display the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner before granting local or remote access to the system via a graphical user login.

| Field | Value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must display the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner before granting local or remote access to the system via a graphical user login.

**Why it matters:** Before anyone can sign in, the computer shows a warning message saying the system belongs to the government, that activity is monitored, and that using it means you agree to that. Think of it like the "this area is under video surveillance" sign at the entrance to a building: it doesn't lock the door, but it makes the rules clear and discourages misuse.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL the banner is typically set in /etc/issue (console and SSH pre-auth via the sshd 'Banner' directive) and in the GNOME login screen via dconf ('banner-message-enable' and 'banner-message-text'). The text must match the DoD standard banner exactly, including line breaks where the check text calls for them.

**Also related (Remote Desktop & Remote Management):** On RHEL, X11 forwarding ('X11Forwarding no' in sshd), VNC servers and cockpit are the main remote-access paths to restrict.

**Operational impact:** No functional impact. Automated logons and kiosk workflows will need to acknowledge the banner, and some scanners compare the text byte-for-byte, so copy it from the STIG rather than retyping it.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, Gnome Shell. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 displays the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner before granting access to the operating system via a graphical user login with the following command:

$ gsettings get org.gnome.login-screen banner-message-text
banner-message-text=
'You are accessing a U.S. Government (USG) Information System (IS) that is provided for USG-authorized use only.\nBy using this IS (which includes any device attached to this IS), you consent to the following conditions:\n-The USG routinely intercepts and monitors communications on this IS for purposes including, but not limited to, penetration testing, COMSEC monitoring, network operations and defense, personnel misconduct (PM), law enforcement (LE), and counterintelligence (CI) investigations.\n-At any time, the USG may inspect and seize data stored on this IS.\n-Communications using, or data stored on, this IS are not private, are subject to routine monitoring, interception, and search, and may be disclosed or used for any USG-authorized purpose.\n-This IS includes security measures (e.g., authentication and access controls) to protect USG interests--not for your personal benefit or privacy.\n-Notwithstanding the above, using this IS does not constitute consent to PM, LE or CI investigative searching or monitoring of the content of privileged communications, or work product, related to personal representation or services by attorneys, psychotherapists, or clergy, and their assistants. Such communications and work product are private and confidential. See User Agreement for details. '

Note: The "\n " characters are for formatting only. They will not be displayed on the graphical interface.

If the banner does not match the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner exactly, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to display the Standard Mandatory DoW Notice and Consent Banner before granting access to the system.

Add the following lines to the [org/gnome/login-screen] section of the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/01-banner-message":

banner-message-text='You are accessing a U.S. Government (USG) Information System (IS) that is provided for USG-authorized use only.\nBy using this IS (which includes any device attached to this IS), you consent to the following conditions:\n-The USG routinely intercepts and monitors communications on this IS for purposes including, but not limited to, penetration testing, COMSEC monitoring, network operations and defense, personnel misconduct (PM), law enforcement (LE), and counterintelligence (CI) investigations.\n-At any time, the USG may inspect and seize data stored on this IS.\n-Communications using, or data stored on, this IS are not private, are subject to routine monitoring, interception, and search, and may be disclosed or used for any USG-authorized purpose.\n-This IS includes security measures (e.g., authentication and access controls) to protect USG interests--not for your personal benefit or privacy.\n-Notwithstanding the above, using this IS does not constitute consent to PM, LE or CI investigative searching or monitoring of the content of privileged communications, or work product, related to personal representation or services by attorneys, psychotherapists, or clergy, and their assistants. Such communications and work product are private and confidential. See User Agreement for details. '

Note: The "\n " characters are for formatting only. They will not be displayed on the graphical interface.

Run the following command to update the database:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Display of a standardized and approved use notification before granting access to the operating system ensures privacy and security notification verbiage used is consistent with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidance.

System use notifications are required only for access via login interfaces with human users and are not required when such human interfaces do not exist.

The banner must be formatted in accordance with applicable DoW policy. Use the following verbiage for operating systems that can accommodate banners of 1300 characters:

"You are accessing a U.S. Government (USG) Information System (IS) that is provided for USG-authorized use only.

By using this IS (which includes any device attached to this IS), you consent to the following conditions:

-The USG routinely intercepts and monitors communications on this IS for purposes including, but not limited to, penetration testing, COMSEC monitoring, network operations and defense, personnel misconduct (PM), law enforcement (LE), and counterintelligence (CI) investigations.

-At any time, the USG may inspect and seize data stored on this IS.

-Communications using, or data stored on, this IS are not private, are subject to routine monitoring, interception, and search, and may be disclosed or used for any USG-authorized purpose.

-This IS includes security measures (e.g., authentication and access controls) to protect USG interests--not for your personal benefit or privacy.

-Notwithstanding the above, using this IS does not constitute consent to PM, LE or CI investigative searching or monitoring of the content of privileged communications, or work product, related to personal representation or services by attorneys, psychotherapists, or clergy, and their assistants. Such communications and work product are private and confidential. See User Agreement for details."

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000023-GPOS-00006, SRG-OS-000228-GPOS-00088

**Threat & control context:** A notice-and-consent banner is a legal and deterrence control rather than a technical barrier. It establishes that users have no expectation of privacy, which supports monitoring, incident response and prosecution, and it satisfies AC-8 (System Use Notification). Assessors verify the exact approved DoD text, that it appears for every access path (console, GUI, SSH and other remote sessions), and that the user must acknowledge it before the session continues.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000048**: Display an organization-defined system use notification message or banner to users before granting access to the system that provides privacy and security notices consistent with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and guidelines.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 a · Rev 4: AC-8 a · Rev 3: AC-8 a
- **CCI-001384**: For publicly accessible systems, display system use information with organization-defined conditions before granting further access to the publicly accessible system.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 c 1 · Rev 4: AC-8 c 1 · Rev 3: AC-8 c
- **CCI-001385**: For publicly accessible systems, displays references, if any, to monitoring that are consistent with privacy accommodations for such systems that generally prohibit those activities.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 c 2 · Rev 4: AC-8 c 2 · Rev 3: AC-8 c
- **CCI-001386**: For publicly accessible systems, displays references, if any, to recording that are consistent with privacy accommodations for such systems that generally prohibit those activities.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 c 2 · Rev 4: AC-8 c 2 · Rev 3: AC-8 c
- **CCI-001387**: For publicly accessible systems, displays references, if any, to auditing that are consistent with privacy accommodations for such systems that generally prohibit those activities.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 c 2 · Rev 4: AC-8 c 2 · Rev 3: AC-8 c
- **CCI-001388**: For publicly accessible systems, includes a description of the authorized uses of the system.  
  Rev 5: AC-8 c 3 · Rev 4: AC-8 c 3 · Rev 3: AC-8 c

#### Level 3: General Audience

/org/gnome/login-screen/banner-message-enable

$ sudo dconf update

It's like a garage where you can store things but nobody is allowed to live.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If no NFS mounts are configured, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 has the "nodev" option configured for all NFS mounts with the following command:

$ sudo grep nfs /etc/fstab
192.168.22.2:/mnt/export /data nfs4 rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,sync,soft,sec=krb5:krb5i:krb5p

If the system is mounting file systems via NFS and the "nodev" option is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent special devices on file systems that are imported via NFS.

Update each NFS mounted file system to use the "nodev" option on file systems that are being imported via NFS.
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nodev" mount option causes the system to not interpret character or block special devices. **Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

### V-281230 · RHEL-10-700110 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent files with the "setuid" and "setgid" bit set from being executed on file systems that are imported via Network File System (NFS).

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281230r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions, File System Layout & Mount Options |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent files with the "setuid" and "setgid" bit set from being executed on file systems that are imported via Network File System (NFS).

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If no NFS mounts are configured, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 has the "nosuid" option configured for all NFS mounts with the following command:

$ sudo grep nfs /etc/fstab
192.168.22.2:/mnt/export /data nfs4 rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,sync,soft,sec=krb5:krb5i:krb5p

If the system is mounting file systems via NFS and the "nosuid" option is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent files with the "setuid" and "setgid" bit set from being executed on file systems that are imported via NFS.

Update each NFS mounted file system to use the "nosuid" option on file systems that are being imported via NFS.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nosuid" mount option causes the system not to execute "setuid" and "setgid" files with owner privileges. This option must be used for mounting any file system not containing approved "setuid" and "setguid" files. Executing files from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281232 · RHEL-10-700120 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must mount "/boot" with the "nodev" option.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281232r1166648_rule` |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must mount "/boot" with the "nodev" option.

**Why it matters:** The computer's storage is divided into separate sections, like rooms in a house. This rule keeps certain rooms separate so one can't overflow into the others, and marks rooms such as the "temporary storage" area as places where programs aren't allowed to run. It's like a garage where you can store things but nobody is allowed to live.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that the "/boot" mount point has the "nodev" option with the following command:

$ mount | grep '\s/boot\s'
/dev/sda1 on /boot type xfs (rw,nodev,nosuid,relatime,seclabel,attr2)

If the "/boot" file system does not have the "nodev" option set, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to mount "/boot" with the "nodev" option.

Modify "/etc/fstab" to use the "nodev" option on the "/boot" directory.

To reload all implicit mount units and update the dependency graph so that new options will apply correctly at next remount, run the following command:

$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload

Use the following command to apply the changes immediately without a reboot:

$ sudo mount -o remount /boot
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The only legitimate location for device files is the "/dev" directory located on the root partition. The only exception to this is chroot jails.

**Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

| SRG | SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154 |
| Topic | File System Layout & Mount Options |
| CCI | CCI-001764 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must mount "/dev/shm" with the "nodev" option.

**Why it matters:** The computer's storage is divided into separate sections, like rooms in a house. This rule keeps certain rooms separate so one can't overflow into the others, and marks rooms such as the "temporary storage" area as places where programs aren't allowed to run. It's like a garage where you can store things but nobody is allowed to live.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that "/dev/shm" is mounted with the "nodev" option with the following command:

$ mount | grep /dev/shm
tmpfs on /dev/shm type tmpfs (rw,nodev,nosuid,noexec,seclabel)

If the "/dev/shm" file system is mounted without the "nodev" option, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to mount "/dev/shm" with the "nodev" option.

Modify "/etc/fstab" to use the "nodev" option on the "/dev/shm" file system.

To reload all implicit mount units and update the dependency graph so that new options will apply correctly at next remount, run the following command:

$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload

Use the following command to apply the changes immediately without a reboot:

$ sudo mount -o remount /dev/shm
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nodev" mount option causes the system to not interpret character or block special devices. Executing character or block special devices from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

The only legitimate location for device files is the "/dev" directory located on the root partition, with the exception of chroot jails if implemented.

**Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281242 · RHEL-10-700170 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must mount "/var/log" with the "nodev" option.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281242r1166678_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154 |
| Topic | File System Layout & Mount Options |
| CCI | CCI-001764 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must mount "/var/log" with the "nodev" option.

**Why it matters:** The computer's storage is divided into separate sections, like rooms in a house. This rule keeps certain rooms separate so one can't overflow into the others, and marks rooms such as the "temporary storage" area as places where programs aren't allowed to run. It's like a garage where you can store things but nobody is allowed to live.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that "/var/log" is mounted with the "nodev" option:

$ mount | grep /var/log
/dev/mapper/luks-c651f493-9fdc-4c6e-a711-0a4f03149661 on /var/log type xfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,seclabel,attr2)

If the "/var/log" file system is mounted without the "nodev" option, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to mount "/var/log" with the "nodev" option.

Modify "/etc/fstab" to use the "nodev" option on the "/var/log" directory.

To reload all implicit mount units and update the dependency graph so that new options will apply correctly at next remount, run the following command:

$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload

Use the following command to apply the changes immediately without a reboot:

$ sudo mount -o remount /var/log
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nodev" mount option causes the system to not interpret character or block special devices. Executing character or block special devices from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

The only legitimate location for device files is the "/dev" directory located on the root partition, with the exception of chroot jails if implemented.

**Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that all nonroot local partitions are mounted with the "nodev" option with the following command:

$ sudo mount | grep '^/dev\S* on /\S' | grep --invert-match 'nodev'

If any output is produced, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that "/etc/fstab" uses the "nodev" option on all nonroot local partitions.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "nodev" mount option causes the system to not interpret character or block special devices. Executing character or block special devices from untrusted file systems increases the opportunity for nonprivileged users to attain unauthorized administrative access.

The only legitimate location for device files is the "/dev" directory located on the root partition, with the exception of chroot jails if implemented.

**Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281249 · RHEL-10-700400 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enable the SELinux targeted policy.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281249r1197242_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000445-GPOS-00199 |
| Topic | Mandatory Access & Application Control |
| CCI | CCI-002696 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enable the SELinux targeted policy.

**Why it matters:** Instead of trying to spot every bad program, the computer keeps a list of approved programs and only those are allowed to run, while each program is kept to its own lane. It's like a guest list at an event: if you're not on the list, you don't get in, no matter how convincing you look.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SELinux*: Security-Enhanced Linux: a strict rulebook that limits what each program is allowed to touch, even if it's running as an administrator.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/selinux/config | SELINUXTYPE | targeted |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set SELinux in /etc/selinux/config ('SELINUX=enforcing', 'SELINUXTYPE=targeted') and verify with 'getenforce' and 'sestatus'. Fix labels with 'restorecon -Rv' and troubleshoot denials with 'ausearch -m AVC' or 'sealert'. fapolicyd ('systemctl enable --now fapolicyd') uses rules in /etc/fapolicyd/rules.d/ and the trust database. Start with 'permissive = 1' to gather data, then enforce.

**Operational impact:** Turning on enforcement without a learning period will block legitimate software. Use permissive or audit mode, analyze the logs, build rules, then enforce. Never disable SELinux to 'fix' an application. Fix the label or policy instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 SELINUX is using the targeted policy with the following command:

$ sestatus | grep policy
Loaded policy name:             targeted

If the loaded policy name is not "targeted", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use the targeted SELINUX policy.

Edit the file "/etc/selinux/config" and add or modify the following line:

SELINUXTYPE=targeted

A reboot is required for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Setting the SELinux policy to "targeted" or a more specialized policy ensures the system will confine processes that are likely to be targeted for exploitation, such as network or system services.

Note: During the development or debugging of SELinux modules, it is common to temporarily place nonproduction systems in "permissive" mode. In such temporary cases, SELinux policies should be developed, and once work is completed, the system should be reconfigured to "targeted".

**Threat & control context:** Discretionary permissions can't stop a compromised process from doing whatever its user can do. Mandatory access control such as SELinux confines each service to its policy, which contains exploitation of daemons. Application allowlisting (fapolicyd, AppLocker, WDAC) implements CM-7(5) (authorized software, deny-by-default) and AC-3(3) (mandatory access control), defeating most commodity malware and unauthorized tools. These are among the highest-value preventive controls in the baseline.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002696**: Verify correct operation of organization-defined security functions.  
  Rev 5: SI-6 a · Rev 4: SI-6 a · Rev 3: n/a
