### V-281250 · RHEL-10-700410 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must elevate the SELinux context when an administrator calls the sudo command.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281250r1184704_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo), Mandatory Access & Application Control |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must elevate the SELinux context when an administrator calls the sudo command.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SELinux*: Security-Enhanced Linux: a strict rulebook that limits what each program is allowed to touch, even if it's running as an administrator.
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Also related (Mandatory Access & Application Control):** On RHEL, set SELinux in /etc/selinux/config ('SELINUX=enforcing', 'SELINUXTYPE=targeted') and verify with 'getenforce' and 'sestatus'. Fix labels with 'restorecon -Rv' and troubleshoot denials with 'ausearch -m AVC' or 'sealert'. fapolicyd ('systemctl enable --now fapolicyd') uses rules in /etc/fapolicyd/rules.d/ and the trust database. Start with 'permissive = 1' to gather data, then enforce.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 elevates the SELinux context when an administrator calls the sudo command with the following command:

This command must be run as root:

$ sudo grep -r sysadm_r /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d
%{designated_group_or_user_name} ALL=(ALL) TYPE=sysadm_t ROLE=sysadm_r ALL

If a designated sudoers administrator group or account(s) is not configured to elevate the SELinux type and role to "sysadm_t" and "sysadm_r" with the use of the sudo command, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to elevate the SELinux context when an administrator calls the sudo command.

Edit a file in the "/etc/sudoers.d" directory with the following command:

$ sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/

Use the following example to build the file in the "/etc/sudoers.d" directory to allow any administrator belonging to a designated sudoers admin group to elevate their SELinux context with the use of the sudo command:

%{designated_group_or_user_name} ALL=(ALL) TYPE=sysadm_t ROLE=sysadm_r ALL

Remove any configurations that conflict with the above from the following locations:

/etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d/
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without verification of the security functions, security functions may not operate correctly and the failure may go unnoticed. Security function is defined as the hardware, software, and/or firmware of the information system responsible for enforcing the system security policy and supporting the isolation of code and data on which the protection is based.

Security functionality includes, but is not limited to, establishing system accounts, configuring access authorizations (i.e., permissions, privileges), setting events to be audited, and setting intrusion detection parameters.

This requirement applies to operating systems performing security function verification/testing and/or systems and environments that require this functionality.

Preventing nonprivileged users from executing privileged functions mitigates the risk that unauthorized individuals or processes may gain unnecessary access to information or privileges.

Privileged functions include, for example, establishing accounts, performing system integrity checks, or administering cryptographic key management activities. Nonprivileged users are individuals who do not possess appropriate authorizations. Circumventing intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms or malicious code protection mechanisms are examples of privileged functions that require protection from nonprivileged users.

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-6 a, SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-3 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must use a Linux Security Module configured to enforce limits on system services.

**Why it matters:** Computers run many background programs ("services") all the time. This rule makes sure the important security ones are always running and the unneeded or risky ones are switched off, like keeping the alarm system armed while unplugging the appliances you don't use.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/selinux/config | SELINUX | enforcing |

**How it works:** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Before masking a service, confirm nothing depends on it ('systemctl list-dependencies --reverse <unit>').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces correct operation of security functions through the use of SELinux with the following command:

$ getenforce
Enforcing

If SELINUX is not set to "Enforcing", this is a finding.

Verify SELinux is configured to be enforcing at boot.

$ sudo grep "SELINUX=" /etc/selinux/config | grep -v '#'
SELINUX=enforcing

If an uncommented SELinux line is missing or not set to "enforcing", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enforce correct operation of security functions.

Edit the file "/etc/selinux/config" and add or modify the following line:

 SELINUX=enforcing

A reboot is required for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without verification of the security functions, security functions may not operate correctly and the failure may go unnoticed. Security function is defined as the hardware, software, and/or firmware of the information system responsible for enforcing the system security policy and supporting the isolation of code and data on which the protection is based.

Security functionality includes, but is not limited to, establishing system accounts, configuring access authorizations (i.e., permissions, privileges), setting events to be audited, and setting intrusion detection parameters.

This requirement applies to operating systems performing security function verification/testing and/or systems and environments that require this functionality.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000445-GPOS-00199, SRG-OS-000134-GPOS-00068

**Threat & control context:** Security functions such as auditd, firewalld, sshd's hardened configuration, fapolicyd and USBGuard only protect the system while their services are running. Conversely, every listening or socket-activated service is reachable attack surface. CM-7 (least functionality) and AU/SI controls require the security services to be enabled and the non-essential ones disabled or masked so they can't be started indirectly.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002696**: Verify correct operation of organization-defined security functions.  
  Rev 5: SI-6 a · Rev 4: SI-6 a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001084**: Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions.  
  Rev 5: SC-3 · Rev 4: SC-3 · Rev 3: SC-3

### V-281252 · RHEL-10-700430 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must configure SELinux context type to allow the use of a nondefault faillock tally directory.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281252r1166708_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Mandatory Access & Application Control |
| CCI | CCI-000044 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting, File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must configure SELinux context type to allow the use of a nondefault faillock tally directory.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SELinux*: Security-Enhanced Linux: a strict rulebook that limits what each program is allowed to touch, even if it's running as an administrator.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/security/faillock.conf | dir | /var/log/faillock |
| Permission | semanage | fcontext -a -t faillog_t "/var/log/faillock(/.*)?" |  |
| Permission | restorecon | -R -v /var/log/faillock |  |

**How it works:** RHEL 8.2+ uses pam_faillock configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, even_deny_root, dir, audit, silent) and wired into system-auth and password-auth by authselect ('authselect enable-feature with-faillock'). Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'. Pointing 'dir' at a persistent path such as /var/log/faillock keeps lockouts across reboots.

**Also related (Mandatory Access & Application Control):** On RHEL, set SELinux in /etc/selinux/config ('SELINUX=enforcing', 'SELINUXTYPE=targeted') and verify with 'getenforce' and 'sestatus'. Fix labels with 'restorecon -Rv' and troubleshoot denials with 'ausearch -m AVC' or 'sealert'. fapolicyd ('systemctl enable --now fapolicyd') uses rules in /etc/fapolicyd/rules.d/ and the trust database. Start with 'permissive = 1' to gather data, then enforce.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If the system does not have SELinux enabled and enforcing a targeted policy, or if the pam_faillock module is not configured for use, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 SELinux context type allows the use of a nondefault faillock tally directory.

Verify the location of the nondefault tally directory for the pam_faillock module with the following command:

$ sudo grep -w dir /etc/security/faillock.conf
dir = /var/log/faillock

Check the security context type of the nondefault tally directory with the following command:

$ ls -Zd /var/log/faillock
unconfined_u:object_r:faillog_t:s0 /var/log/faillock

If the security context type of the nondefault tally directory is not "faillog_t", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to allow the use of a nondefault faillock tally directory while SELinux enforces a targeted policy.

Enable the feature using the following command:

$ sudo authselect enable-feature with-faillock

Create a nondefault faillock tally directory (if it does not already exist) with the following example:

$ sudo mkdir /var/log/faillock

Add/modify the "/etc/security/faillock.conf" file to match the following line:

dir = /var/log/faillock

Update "/etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts.local" with "faillog_t" context type for the nondefault faillock tally directory with the following command:

$ sudo semanage fcontext -a -t faillog_t "/var/log/faillock(/.*)?"

Update the context type of the nondefault faillock directory/subdirectories and files with the following command:

$ sudo restorecon -R -v /var/log/faillock
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Not having the correct SELinux context on the faillock directory may lead to unauthorized access to the directory.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a

### V-281253 · RHEL-10-700500 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured so that Secure Shell (SSH) public host key files have mode "0644" or less permissive.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281253r1184654_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000445-GPOS-00199 |
| Topic | SSH Remote Administration, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-002696 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that Secure Shell (SSH) public host key files have mode "0644" or less permissive.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | 0644 /etc/ssh/*key.pub |  |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 SSH public host key files have a mode of "0644" or less permissive with the following command:

Note: SSH public key files may be found in other directories on the system depending on the installation.

$ sudo stat -c "%a %n" /etc/ssh/*.pub
644 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_dsa_key.pub
644 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ecdsa_key.pub
644 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
644 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub

If any "key.pub" file has a mode more permissive than "0644", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 SSH public host key files to have mode "0644" or less permissive.

Change the mode of public host key files under "/etc/ssh" to "0644" with the following command:

$ sudo chmod 0644 /etc/ssh/*key.pub

Restart the SSH daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If a public host key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002696**: Verify correct operation of organization-defined security functions.  
  Rev 5: SI-6 a · Rev 4: SI-6 a · Rev 3: n/a

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d | GSSAPIAuthentication | no |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 SSH daemons do not allow GSSAPI authentication with the following command:

$ sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -dd 2>&1 | awk '/filename/ {print $4}' | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' ' | xargs sudo grep -iH '^\s*gssapiauthentication'
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-stig.conf:GSSAPIAuthentication no
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-redhat.conf:GSSAPIAuthentication yes

Verify the runtime setting with the following command:

$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i gssapiauthentication
gssapiauthentication no

If the "GSSAPIAuthentication" keyword is not set to "no" in a drop-in that lexicographically precedes 50-redhat.conf, no output is returned, and the use of GSSAPI authentication has not been documented with the information system security officer, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 SSH daemons to not allow GSSAPI authentication.

In "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d", create a drop file that will lexicographically precede 50-redhat.conf and add the following line:

GSSAPIAuthentication no

Restart the SSH service with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** GSSAPI authentication is used to provide additional authentication mechanisms to applications. Allowing GSSAPI authentication through SSH exposes the system's GSSAPI to remote hosts, increasing the attack surface of the system.

OpenSSH uses the first occurrence of a keyword it sees, and drop-in files are read in lexicographical order at the start of the configuration. Red Hat recommends using drop-in files rather than changing base configuration files.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

  Rev 5: CM-5 (1) (a) · Rev 4: CM-5 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |

```text
Verify the runtime setting with the following command:

$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i printlastlog

If the "PrintLastLog" keyword is not set to "yes" in a drop-in that lexicographically precedes 50-redhat.conf, or if no output is returned, this is a finding.
```

```text

In "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d", create a drop file that will lexicographically precede 50-redhat.conf and add the following line:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that Secure Shell (SSH) server configuration files' permissions are not modified.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that SSH server configuration files' permissions are not modified.

Check the permissions of the "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" file with the following command:

$ sudo rpm --verify openssh-server | awk '! ($2 == "c" && $1 ~ /^.\..\.\.\.\..\./) {print $0}'

If the command returns any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that SSH server configuration files' permissions are not modified.

Run the following commands to restore the correct permissions of OpenSSH server configuration files:

$ sudo rpm --setugids openssh-server
$ sudo rpm --setperms openssh-server
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Service configuration files enable or disable features of their respective services, which if configured incorrectly can lead to insecure and vulnerable configurations. Therefore, service configuration files must be owned by the correct group to prevent unauthorized changes.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d | PermitEmptyPasswords | no |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

```text
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-stig.conf:PermitEmptyPasswords no

Verify the runtime setting with the following command:

$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i permitemptypasswords
permitemptypasswords no

If the "PermitEmptyPasswords" keyword is not set to "no" in a drop-in that lexicographically precedes 50-redhat.conf, or if no output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent SSH users from logging on with blank passwords.

In "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d", create a drop file that will lexicographically precede 50-redhat.conf and add the following line:

PermitEmptyPasswords no

Restart the SSH daemon with the following command for the settings to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d | PermitRootLogin | no |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening):** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 remote access using SSH prevents users from logging on directly as "root" with the following command:

$ sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -dd 2>&1 | awk '/filename/ {print $4}' | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' ' | xargs sudo grep -iH '^\s*permitrootlogin'
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-stig.conf:PermitRootLogin no

Verify the runtime setting with the following command:

$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i permitrootlogin
permitrootlogin no

If the "PermitRootLogin" keyword is not set to "no" in a drop-in that lexicographically precedes 50-redhat.conf, or if no output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent SSH users from logging on directly as root.

In "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d", create a drop-in file that will lexicographically precede 50-redhat.conf and add the following line:

PermitRootLogin no

Restart the SSH daemon with the following command for the settings to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Even though the communications channel may be encrypted, an additional layer of security is gained by extending the policy of not logging directly on as root. In addition, logging in with a user-specific account provides individual accountability of actions performed on the system and helps to minimize direct attack attempts on root's password.

OpenSSH uses the first occurrence of a keyword it sees, and drop-in files are read in lexicographical order at the start of the configuration. Red Hat recommends using drop-in files rather than changing base configuration files.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004045**: Require users to be individually authenticated before granting access to the shared accounts or resources.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (5) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

```text
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-stig.conf:HostbasedAuthentication no

Verify the runtime setting with the following command:

$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i hostbasedauthentication
hostbasedauthentication no

If the "HostbasedAuthentication" keyword is not set to "no" in a drop-in that lexicographically precedes 50-redhat.conf, or no output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text

In "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d", create a drop file that will lexicographically precede 50-redhat.conf and add the following line:

```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** SSH trust relationships mean a compromise on one host can allow an attacker to move trivially to other hosts.

OpenSSH uses the first occurrence of a keyword it sees, and drop-in files are read in lexicographical order at the start of the configuration. Red Hat recommends using drop-in files rather than changing base configuration files.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. #### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that all network connections associated with Secure Shell (SSH) traffic terminate after becoming unresponsive.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d | ClientAliveCountMax | 1 |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. **Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 network connections associated with SSH traffic terminate after becoming unresponsive.

Set the "ClientAliveCountMax" to "1" by performing the following command:

$ sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -dd 2>&1 | awk '/filename/ {print $4}' | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' ' | xargs sudo grep -iH '^\s*clientalivecountmax'
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-stig.conf:ClientAliveCountMax 1

```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to automatically terminate all network connections associated with SSH traffic at the end of a session or after 10 minutes of inactivity.

In "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d", create a drop file that will lexicographically precede 50-redhat.conf and add the following line:

ClientAliveCountMax 1

Restart the SSH daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Terminating an idle SSH session within a short time period reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized personnel to take control of a management session enabled on the console or console port that has been left unattended. Quickly terminating an idle SSH session will also free up resources committed by the managed network element.

Terminating network connections associated with communications sessions includes, for example, deallocating associated TCP/IP address/port pairs at the operating system level and deallocating networking assignments at the application level if multiple application sessions are using a single operating system-level network connection. This does not mean the operating system terminates all sessions or network access; it only ends the inactive session and releases the resources associated with that session.

RHEL 10 uses "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" for configurations of OpenSSH. Within the sshd_config, the product of the values of "ClientAliveInterval" and "ClientAliveCountMax" are used to establish the inactivity threshold. The "ClientAliveInterval" is a timeout interval in seconds after which if no data has been received from the client, sshd will send a message through the encrypted channel to request a response from the client. The "ClientAliveCountMax" is the number of client alive messages that may be sent without sshd receiving any messages back from the client. If this threshold is met, sshd will disconnect the client. For more information on these settings and others, refer to the sshd_config man pages.

OpenSSH uses the first occurrence of a keyword it sees, and drop-in files are read in lexicographical order at the start of the configuration. Red Hat recommends using drop-in files rather than changing base configuration files.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

  Rev 5: SC-10 · Rev 4: SC-10 · Rev 3: SC-10
- **CCI-002361**: Automatically terminate a user session after organization-defined conditions or trigger events requiring session disconnect.  
  Rev 5: AC-12 · Rev 4: AC-12 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281270 · RHEL-10-700670 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must forward mail from postmaster to the root account using a postfix alias.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281270r1166762_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000046-GPOS-00022 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening, Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-000139 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-5 a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must forward mail from postmaster to the root account using a postfix alias.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, root logon is controlled through sshd ('PermitRootLogin no'), /etc/securetty (where present), and PAM. Empty passwords are blocked by removing 'nullok' from pam_unix in system-auth and password-auth and by setting 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd. Only root should have UID 0 ('awk -F: "$3==0" /etc/passwd').

**Also related (Network Stack Hardening):** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 notifies administrators in the event of an audit processing failure.

Check that the "/etc/aliases" file has a defined value for "root".

$ sudo grep "postmaster:\s*root$" /etc/aliases
postmaster:     root

If the command does not return a line, or the line is commented out, ask the system administrator to indicate how they and the information systems security officer are notified of an audit process failure.

If there is no evidence of the proper personnel being notified of an audit processing failure, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to have a valid email address as an alias for the root account.

Append the following line to "/etc/aliases":

postmaster: root

Run the following command:

$ sudo newaliases
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** It is critical for the appropriate personnel to be aware if a system is at risk of failing to process audit logs as required. Without this notification, the security personnel may be unaware of an impending failure of the audit capability, and system operation may be adversely affected.

Audit processing failures include software/hardware errors, failures in the audit capturing mechanisms, and audit storage capacity being reached or exceeded.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000139**: Alert organization-defined personnel or roles within an organization-defined time period in the event of an audit logging process failure.  
  Rev 5: AU-5 a · Rev 4: AU-5 a · Rev 3: AU-5 a

### V-281271 · RHEL-10-700680 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must not have a "shosts.equiv" file on the system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281271r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | SSH Remote Administration |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not have a "shosts.equiv" file on the system.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 does not have a "shosts.equiv" file on the system with the following command:

$ sudo find / -name shosts.equiv

If a "shosts.equiv" file is found, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to not have a "shosts.equiv" file on the system.

Remove any found "shosts.equiv" files from the system:

$ sudo rm /[path]/[to]/[file]/shosts.equiv
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The "shosts.equiv" files are used to configure host-based authentication for the system via Secure Shell (SSH). Host-based authentication is not sufficient for preventing unauthorized access to the system, as it does not require interactive identification and authentication of a connection request, or for the use of two-factor authentication.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

---

### V-281273 · RHEL-10-700700 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent a user from overriding the disabling of the graphical user interface automount function.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281273r1184699_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000114-GPOS-00059 |
| Topic | File System Layout & Mount Options, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000778, CCI-001958 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-3 |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent a user from overriding the disabling of the graphical user interface automount function.

**Why it matters:** The computer's storage is divided into separate sections, like rooms in a house. This rule keeps certain rooms separate so one can't overflow into the others, and marks rooms such as the "temporary storage" area as places where programs aren't allowed to run. It's like a garage where you can store things but nobody is allowed to live.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock | /org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/automount-open | locked |

**How it works:** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 disables the ability of the user to override the graphical user interface automount setting.

Determine which profile the system database is using with the following command:

$ sudo grep system-db /etc/dconf/profile/user
system-db:local

Check that the automount setting is locked from nonprivileged user modification with the following command:

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system, so the path is "/etc/dconf/db/local.d". This path must be modified if a database other than "local" is being used.

$ sudo grep 'automount-open' /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/*
/org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/automount-open

If the command does not return at least the example result, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that the GNOME desktop does not allow a user to change the setting that disables automated mounting of removable media.

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system. If the system is using another database in "/etc/dconf/profile/user", the file should be created under the appropriate subdirectory.

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock" file to prevent user modification:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock

/org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/automount-open

Update the dconf system databases:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without identifying and authenticating devices, unidentified or unknown devices may be introduced, thereby facilitating malicious activity.

Peripherals include, but are not limited to, such devices as flash drives, external storage, and printers.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000114-GPOS-00059, SRG-OS-000378-GPOS-00163

**Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service; T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000778**: Uniquely identify organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: IA-3
- **CCI-001958**: Authenticate organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281274 · RHEL-10-700710 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent a user from overriding the disabling of the graphical user interface autorun function.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281274r1197245_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000114-GPOS-00059 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000778, CCI-001958 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-3 |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent a user from overriding the disabling of the graphical user interface autorun function.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock | /org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/autorun-never | locked |

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel modules are blocked by adding 'install usb-storage /bin/false' and 'blacklist usb-storage' to /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf (similar entries for bluetooth and firewire-core). USBGuard ('dnf install usbguard', policy in /etc/usbguard/rules.conf, generated with 'usbguard generate-policy') allowlists permitted devices. Wireless interfaces are disabled with 'nmcli radio all off'.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 disables ability of the user to override the graphical user interface autorun setting.

Check that the autorun setting is set to prevent user modification with the following command:

$ gsettings writable org.gnome.desktop.media-handling autorun-never
false

If "autorun-never" is writable, the result is "true".

If this is not documented with the information system security officer as an operational requirement, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that the GNOME desktop does not allow a user to change the setting that disables autorun on removable media.

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system. If the system is using another database in "/etc/dconf/profile/user", the file should be created under the appropriate subdirectory.

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock" file to prevent user modification:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock

/org/gnome/desktop/media-handling/autorun-never

Update the dconf system databases:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Techniques used to address this include protocols using nonces (e.g., numbers generated for a specific one-time use) or challenges (e.g., Transport Layer Security [TLS], WS_Security). Additional techniques include time-synchronous or challenge-response one-time authenticators.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000114-GPOS-00059, SRG-OS-000378-GPOS-00163

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000778**: Uniquely identify organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: IA-3
- **CCI-001958**: Authenticate organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281275 · RHEL-10-700720 · CAT I: RHEL 10 must not allow unattended or automatic login via the graphical user interface.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281275r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not allow unattended or automatic login via the graphical user interface.

**Why it matters:** This decides what the sign-in screen shows and which shortcuts are allowed. For example, it hides the list of usernames, doesn't show who signed in last, and turns off "sign in automatically". It's like a hotel front desk that won't tell a stranger which room a guest is in.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/gdm/custom.conf | AutomaticLoginEnable | false |

**How it works:** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** Users will need to type their username in full and can't use convenience sign-in methods. Hiding restart buttons on the logon screen means console users need credentials to reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 does not allow an unattended or automatic login to the system via a graphical user interface.

Check for the value of the "AutomaticLoginEnable" in the "/etc/gdm/custom.conf" file with the following command:

$  grep -i automaticlogin /etc/gdm/custom.conf
AutomaticLoginEnable=false

If the value of "AutomaticLoginEnable" is not set to "false", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that the GNOME desktop display manager disables automatic login.

Update the "/etc/gdm/custom.conf" file to disable automatic login to the GNOME desktop:

$ sudo vi /etc/gdm/custom.conf

[daemon]
AutomaticLoginEnable=false
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Failure to restrict system access to authenticated users negatively impacts operating system security.

**Threat & control context:** The logon surface can leak information (usernames, the last logged-on user, local administrator lists) that cuts an attacker's effort in half, and convenience features (automatic logon, picture passwords, convenience PINs, password reveal buttons) weaken authentication assurance. These settings reduce information disclosure (AC-14, IA-6 authenticator feedback) and keep interactive logon on approved authenticators.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281276 · RHEL-10-700730 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent a user from overriding the disabling of the graphical user smart card removal action.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281276r1166780_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000028-GPOS-00009 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout, Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000056, CCI-000057 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-11 b, AC-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-11 b, AC-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-11 b, AC-11 a |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent a user from overriding the disabling of the graphical user smart card removal action.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.
- *Smart card / CAC*: A government ID card with a chip that is used, together with a PIN, to sign in.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock | /org/gnome/settings-daemon/peripherals/smartcard/removal-action | locked |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set GNOME locking through dconf in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/ (org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900, org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, lock-delay=uint32 5) and lock each key in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/ so users can't override it. Then run 'dconf update'. For terminals, set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. Network and SSH sessions use ClientAliveInterval/CountMax and systemd-logind StopIdleSessionSec.

**Also related (Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication):** On RHEL, smart card login is handled by SSSD with 'pam_cert_auth = True', the certificate trust store configured in sssd.conf / /etc/sssd/pki/sssd_auth_ca_db.pem, and certificate mapping rules (matchrule/maprule). Revocation checking is configured with 'certificate_verification' (OCSP). authselect features such as 'with-smartcard' wire SSSD into PAM.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 disables ability of the user to override the smart card removal action setting with the following command:

$ gsettings writable org.gnome.settings-daemon.peripherals.smartcard removal-action
false

If "removal-action" is writable and the result is "true", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent a user from overriding the disabling of the graphical user smart card removal action.

Add the following line to "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock" to prevent user override of the smart card removal action:

/org/gnome/settings-daemon/peripherals/smartcard/removal-action

Update the dconf system databases:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A session lock is a temporary action taken when a user stops work and moves away from the immediate physical vicinity of the information system but does not want to log out because of the temporary nature of the absence.

The session lock is implemented at the point where session activity can be determined. Rather than be forced to wait for a period of time to expire before the user session can be locked, RHEL 10 must provide users with the ability to manually invoke a session lock so users can secure their session if they must temporarily vacate the immediate physical vicinity.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000028-GPOS-00009, SRG-OS-000030-GPOS-00011

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000056**: Retain the device lock until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 b · Rev 4: AC-11 b · Rev 3: AC-11 b
- **CCI-000057**: Prevent further access to the system by initiating a device lock after organization-defined time period of inactivity; and/or requiring the user to initiate a device lock before leaving the system unattended.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 a · Rev 4: AC-11 a · Rev 3: AC-11 a

### V-281277 · RHEL-10-700740 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent a user from overriding the screensaver lock-enabled setting for the graphical user interface.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281277r1166783_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000028-GPOS-00009 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000056, CCI-000057 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-11 b, AC-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-11 b, AC-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-11 b, AC-11 a |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent a user from overriding the screensaver lock-enabled setting for the graphical user interface.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/session | /org/gnome/desktop/screensaver/lock-enabled | locked |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set GNOME locking through dconf in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/ (org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900, org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, lock-delay=uint32 5) and lock each key in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/ so users can't override it. Then run 'dconf update'. For terminals, set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. Network and SSH sessions use ClientAliveInterval/CountMax and systemd-logind StopIdleSessionSec.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, Gnome Shell. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 prevents a user from overriding the screensaver lock-enabled setting with the following command:

$ gsettings writable org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled
false

If "lock-enabled" is writable, and the result is "true", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent a user from overriding settings for graphical user interfaces.

Create a database to contain the systemwide screensaver settings (if it does not already exist) with the following command:

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system. If the system is using another database in "/etc/dconf/profile/user", the file should be created under the appropriate subdirectory.

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/session" file to prevent nonprivileged users from modifying the screensaver lock:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/session

/org/gnome/desktop/screensaver/lock-enabled

Run the following command to update the database:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A session timeout lock is a temporary action taken when a user stops work and moves away from the immediate physical vicinity of the information system but does not log out because of the temporary nature of the absence. Rather than relying on the user to manually lock their operating system session prior to vacating the vicinity, operating systems must be able to identify when a user's session has idled and take action to initiate the session lock.

The session lock is implemented at the point where session activity can be determined and/or controlled.

Implementing session settings will have little value if a user is able to manipulate these settings from the defaults prescribed in the other requirements of this implementation guide.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000028-GPOS-00009, SRG-OS-000030-GPOS-00011

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1087 Account Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000056**: Retain the device lock until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 b · Rev 4: AC-11 b · Rev 3: AC-11 b
- **CCI-000057**: Prevent further access to the system by initiating a device lock after organization-defined time period of inactivity; and/or requiring the user to initiate a device lock before leaving the system unattended.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 a · Rev 4: AC-11 a · Rev 3: AC-11 a

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | [org/gnome/desktop/session] | idle-delay | uint32 600 |

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 initiates a session lock after a 10-minute period of inactivity for graphical user interfaces with the following command:

$ sudo gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.session idle-delay
uint32 600

If "idle-delay" is set to "0" or a value greater than "600", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to initiate a screensaver after a 10-minute period of inactivity for graphical user interfaces.

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-screensaver

[org/gnome/desktop/session]
# Set the lock time out to 900 seconds before the session is considered idle
idle-delay=uint32 600

Update the system databases:

$ sudo dconf update
```
