### V-281282 · RHEL-10-700790 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must conceal, via the session lock, information previously visible on the display with a publicly viewable image.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281282r1166798_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000031-GPOS-00012 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-000060 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-11 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-11 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-11 (1) |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must conceal, via the session lock, information previously visible on the display with a publicly viewable image.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | [org/gnome/desktop/screensaver] | picture-uri | '' |
| dconf | /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock | /org/gnome/desktop/screensaver/picture-uri | locked |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set GNOME locking through dconf in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/ (org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900, org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, lock-delay=uint32 5) and lock each key in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/ so users can't override it. Then run 'dconf update'. For terminals, set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. Network and SSH sessions use ClientAliveInterval/CountMax and systemd-logind StopIdleSessionSec.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 prevents a user from overriding settings a blank screensaver with the following command:

$ gsettings writable org.gnome.desktop.screensaver picture-uri
false

If "picture-uri" is writable, and the result is "true", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent a user from overriding the picture-uri setting for graphical user interfaces.

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system. If the system is using another database in "/etc/dconf/profile/user", the file should be created under the appropriate subdirectory.

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-security-settings" file to prevent a user from overriding the "picture-uri" setting:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-security-settings

[org/gnome/desktop/screensaver]
picture-uri=''

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock" file to prevent a user from modifying the lock applied to the "picture-uri" setting:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/00-security-settings-lock

/org/gnome/desktop/screensaver/picture-uri

Update the dconf system databases:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Setting the screensaver mode to blank-only conceals the contents of the display from passersby.

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000060**: Conceal, via the device lock, information previously visible on the display with a publicly viewable image.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 (1) · Rev 4: AC-11 (1) · Rev 3: AC-11 (1)

### V-281283 · RHEL-10-700800 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must ensure effective dconf policy matches the policy keyfiles.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281283r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must ensure effective dconf policy matches the policy keyfiles.

**Why it matters:** This decides what the sign-in screen shows and which shortcuts are allowed. For example, it hides the list of usernames, doesn't show who signed in last, and turns off "sign in automatically". It's like a hotel front desk that won't tell a stranger which room a guest is in.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** Users will need to type their username in full and can't use convenience sign-in methods. Hiding restart buttons on the logon screen means console users need credentials to reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 ensures effective dconf policy matches the policy keyfiles.

Check the last modification time of the local databases, comparing it to the last modification time of the related keyfiles. The following command will check every dconf database and compare its modification time to the related system keyfiles:

$ function dconf_needs_update { for db in $(find /etc/dconf/db -maxdepth 1 -type f); do db_mtime=$(stat -c %Y "$db"); keyfile_mtime=$(stat -c %Y "$db".d/* | sort -n | tail -1); if [ -n "$db_mtime" ] && [ -n "$keyfile_mtime" ] && [ "$db_mtime" -lt "$keyfile_mtime" ]; then echo "$db needs update"; return 1; fi; done; }; dconf_needs_update

If the command has any output, then a dconf database needs to be updated, and this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to ensure that the effective dconf policy matches the policy keyfiles.

Update the dconf databases by running the following command:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unlike text-based keyfiles, the binary database is impossible to check through most automated and all manual means; therefore, to evaluate dconf configuration, both must be true at the same time. Configuration files must be compliant, and the database must be more recent than those keyfiles, which gives confidence that it reflects them.

**Threat & control context:** The logon surface can leak information (usernames, the last logged-on user, local administrator lists) that cuts an attacker's effort in half, and convenience features (automatic logon, picture passwords, convenience PINs, password reveal buttons) weaken authentication assurance. These settings reduce information disclosure (AC-14, IA-6 authenticator feedback) and keep interactive logon on approved authenticators.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-281285 · RHEL-10-700820 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent a user from overriding the Ctrl-Alt-Del sequence settings for the graphical user interface.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281285r1197249_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186 |
| Topic | Boot Process & Console Security, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-002385 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-5 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent a user from overriding the Ctrl-Alt-Del sequence settings for the graphical user interface.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/session | /org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys/logout | locked |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set the GRUB2 superuser password with 'grub2-setpassword' (stored hashed in /boot/grub2/user.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/user.cfg) and set a unique superuser name in /etc/grub.d/01_users. Rescue and emergency modes must require root authentication (sulogin in rescue.service and emergency.service). Mask Ctrl-Alt-Del with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none' in systemd's system.conf. Mask debug-shell. kdump is disabled unless it's needed.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 users cannot enable the Ctrl-Alt-Del sequence in the GNOME desktop:

$ gsettings writable org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.media-keys logout
false

If "logout" is writable and the result is "true", this is a finding.

If GNOME is configured to shut down when Ctrl-Alt-Del is pressed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to disallow the user changing the Ctrl-Alt-Del sequence in the GNOME desktop.

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system. If the system is using another database in "/etc/dconf/profile/user", the file should be created under the appropriate subdirectory.

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/session" file to prevent nonprivileged users from modifying the Ctrl-Alt-Del setting:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/session

/org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys/logout

Run the following command to update the database:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A locally logged-in user who presses Ctrl-Alt-Del when at the console can reboot the system. If accidentally pressed, as could happen in the case of a mixed operating system environment, this can create the risk of short-term loss of systems' availability due to unintentional reboot.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot; T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281286 · RHEL-10-700830 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must disable the ability of a user to accidentally press Ctrl-Alt-Del and cause a system to shut down or reboot.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281286r1166810_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication, Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-002385 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-5 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable the ability of a user to accidentally press Ctrl-Alt-Del and cause a system to shut down or reboot.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | [org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys] | logout | @as [] |

**How it works:** On RHEL, smart card login is handled by SSSD with 'pam_cert_auth = True', the certificate trust store configured in sssd.conf / /etc/sssd/pki/sssd_auth_ca_db.pem, and certificate mapping rules (matchrule/maprule). Revocation checking is configured with 'certificate_verification' (OCSP). authselect features such as 'with-smartcard' wire SSSD into PAM.

**Also related (Boot Process & Console Security):** On RHEL, set the GRUB2 superuser password with 'grub2-setpassword' (stored hashed in /boot/grub2/user.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/user.cfg) and set a unique superuser name in /etc/grub.d/01_users. Rescue and emergency modes must require root authentication (sulogin in rescue.service and emergency.service). Mask Ctrl-Alt-Del with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none' in systemd's system.conf. Mask debug-shell. kdump is disabled unless it's needed.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 is configured to ignore the Ctrl-Alt-Del sequence in the GNOME desktop with the following command:

Check that the Ctrl-Alt-Del sequence settings for the graphical user interface cannot be overridden with the following command:

$ gsettings get org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.media-keys logout
@as []

If the GNOME desktop is configured to shut down when Ctrl-Alt-Del is pressed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to ignore the Ctrl-Alt-Del sequence in the GNOME desktop.

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system. If the system is using another database in "/etc/dconf/profile/user", the file should be created under the appropriate subdirectory.

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-media-keys" file to set the media-keys logout setting as an empty string array:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-media-keys

[org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys]
logout=@as []

Run the following command to update the database:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A locally logged-in user who presses Ctrl-Alt-Del, when at the console, can reboot the system. If accidentally pressed, as could happen in the case of mixed operating system environments, this can create the risk of short-term loss of availability of systems due to unintentional reboot.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process; T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a

| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-3 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to disable USB mass storage.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *USB*: The common plug used for thumb drives, keyboards and many other devices.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf | blacklist | usb-storage |

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel modules are blocked by adding 'install usb-storage /bin/false' and 'blacklist usb-storage' to /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf (similar entries for bluetooth and firewire-core). USBGuard ('dnf install usbguard', policy in /etc/usbguard/rules.conf, generated with 'usbguard generate-policy') allowlists permitted devices. Wireless interfaces are disabled with 'nmcli radio all off'.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 disables the ability to load the USB Storage kernel module with the following command:

$ sudo grep -rs usb-storage /etc/modprobe.conf /etc/modprobe.d/*
/etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf:install usb-storage /bin/false
/etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf:blacklist usb-storage

If the command does not return any output, or either line is commented out, and use of USB Storage is not documented with the information system security officer as an operational requirement, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent the usb-storage kernel module from being loaded.

Add the following lines to the file "/etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf" (or create "usb-storage.conf" if it does not exist):

$ sudo vi /etc/modprobe.d/usb-storage.conf

install usb-storage /bin/false
blacklist usb-storage
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** USB mass storage permits easy introduction of unknown devices, thereby facilitating malicious activity.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000114-GPOS-00059, SRG-OS-000378-GPOS-00163

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000778**: Uniquely identify organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: IA-3
- **CCI-001958**: Authenticate organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281291 · RHEL-10-700880 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must disable the graphical user interface automounter unless required.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281291r1166825_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000114-GPOS-00059 |
| Topic | File System Layout & Mount Options, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000778, CCI-001958 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-3 |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable the graphical user interface automounter unless required.

**Why it matters:** The computer's storage is divided into separate sections, like rooms in a house. This rule keeps certain rooms separate so one can't overflow into the others, and marks rooms such as the "temporary storage" area as places where programs aren't allowed to run. It's like a garage where you can store things but nobody is allowed to live.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | [org/gnome/desktop/media-handling] | automount-open | false |

**How it works:** On RHEL, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** 'noexec' on /tmp can break installers and tools that extract and run helpers there. Set TMPDIR to an alternate location for those. Re-partitioning a running system is disruptive, so build the layout into the kickstart profile instead.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: This requirement assumes the use of the RHEL 10 default graphical user interface, the GNOME desktop environment. If the system does not have any graphical user interface installed, this requirement is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 disables the graphical user interface automount function.

Disable the setting with the following command:

$ gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.media-handling automount-open
false

If "automount-open" is set to "true" and is not documented with the information system security officer as an operational requirement, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 GNOME to disable automated mount of removable media.

Note: The example below is using the database "local" for the system. If the system is using another database in "/etc/dconf/profile/user", the file should be created under the appropriate subdirectory.

Update the "/etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-security-settings" database file with the following lines:

$ sudo vi /etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-security-settings

[org/gnome/desktop/media-handling]
automount-open=false

Update the dconf system databases:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Automatically mounting file systems permits easy introduction of unknown devices, thereby facilitating malicious activity.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000114-GPOS-00059, SRG-OS-000378-GPOS-00163

**Threat & control context:** Separate partitions keep runaway logs or user data from exhausting the root file system, which is an availability and audit-integrity concern (AU-4, SC-5). Mount options remove whole classes of attack. 'nodev' blocks device files, 'nosuid' neutralizes planted SUID binaries, and 'noexec' prevents execution from world-writable locations such as /tmp and /dev/shm, a common staging area for exploits (CM-6, CM-7).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service; T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000778**: Uniquely identify organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: IA-3
- **CCI-001958**: Authenticate organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281293 · RHEL-10-700900 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must implement nonexecutable data to protect its memory from unauthorized code execution.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281293r1166831_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000433-GPOS-00192 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations |
| CCI | CCI-002824 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-16 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-16 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must implement nonexecutable data to protect its memory from unauthorized code execution.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Boot loader (GRUB)*: The small program that starts the operating system when the computer powers on.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel tunables are set in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf (applied with 'sysctl --system' and verified with 'sysctl <key>'). Remember that a later file or /etc/sysctl.conf can override an earlier drop-in, and the STIG check typically greps all locations for conflicts. Boot parameters (e.g. 'vsyscall=none', 'page_poison=1', 'pti=on', 'slub_debug=P', 'audit=1') are set with 'grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=...'. Core dumps are controlled through /etc/systemd/coredump.conf and 'ulimit -c'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 implements nonexecutable data to protect its memory from unauthorized code execution.

Run the following command:

$ sudo grep ^flags /proc/cpuinfo | grep -Ev '([^[:alnum:]])(nx)([^[:alnum:]]|$)'

If any output is returned, this is a finding.

Run the following command:

$ sudo grubby --info=ALL | grep args | grep -E '([^[:alnum:]])(noexec)([^[:alnum:]])'

If any output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to implement nonexecutable data to protect its memory from unauthorized code execution.

Update the GRUB 2 bootloader configuration.

Run the following command:

$ sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --remove-args=noexec
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** ExecShield uses the segmentation feature on all x86 systems to prevent execution in memory higher than a certain address. It writes an address as a limit in the code segment descriptor, to control where code can be executed, on a per-process basis. When the kernel places a process's memory regions such as the stack and heap higher than this address, the hardware prevents execution in that address range. This is enabled by default on the latest Red Hat and Fedora systems if supported by the hardware.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002824**: Implement organization-defined controls to protect the system memory from unauthorized code execution.  
  Rev 5: SI-16 · Rev 4: SI-16 · Rev 3: n/a

| CCI | CCI-001133 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-10 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-10 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-10 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically exit interactive command shell user sessions after 10 minutes of inactivity.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/profile.d/tmout.sh | declare | -xr TMOUT=600 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set GNOME locking through dconf in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/ (org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900, org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, lock-delay=uint32 5) and lock each key in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/locks/ so users can't override it. Then run 'dconf update'. For terminals, set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. Network and SSH sessions use ClientAliveInterval/CountMax and systemd-logind StopIdleSessionSec.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to exit interactive command shell user sessions after 10 minutes of inactivity or less with the following command:

$ sudo grep -i tmout /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/*.sh
/etc/profile.d/tmout.sh:declare -xr TMOUT=600

If "TMOUT" is not set to "600" or less in a script located in the "/etc/'profile.d/" directory, is missing, or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to exit interactive command shell user sessions after 10 minutes of inactivity.

Add or edit the following line in "/etc/profile.d/tmout.sh":

#!/bin/bash

declare -xr TMOUT=600
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Terminating an idle interactive command shell user session within a short time period reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized personnel to take control of it when left unattended in a virtual terminal or physical console.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000163-GPOS-00072, SRG-OS-000029-GPOS-00010

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001133**: Terminate the network connection associated with a communications session at the end of the session or after an organization-defined time period of inactivity.  
  Rev 5: SC-10 · Rev 4: SC-10 · Rev 3: SC-10

### V-281296 · RHEL-10-700930 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured with a timeout interval for the Secure Shell (SSH) daemon.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281296r1184670_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000163-GPOS-00072 |
| Topic | SSH Remote Administration, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-001133, CCI-002361, CCI-002891 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-10, AC-12, MA-4 (7) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-10, AC-12, MA-4 (7) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-10 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured with a timeout interval for the Secure Shell (SSH) daemon.

**Why it matters:** SSH is the secure "remote control" administrators use to manage the computer over the network by typing commands. This rule tightens how that remote control works: who may use it, how they prove their identity, and how idle connections are closed. It's like making sure the building's service entrance has a good lock and isn't propped open.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d | ClientAliveInterval | 600 |

**How it works:** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and on RHEL 9/10 also drop-ins under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ that are processed in lexical order, where the first value obtained wins. Put STIG settings in an early-sorting drop-in (e.g. 00-stig.conf) so a vendor file can't silently override them. Validate syntax with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload sshd'.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Keep an existing session open while you reload sshd so a typo can't lock you out. Disabling root login requires named admin accounts plus sudo. Idle timeouts (ClientAliveInterval/CountMax) will disconnect long-running interactive sessions, so use tmux or screen for those.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured with an SSH timeout interval.

Verify the "ClientAliveInterval" variable is set to a value of "600" or less by performing the following command:

$ sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -dd 2>&1 | awk '/filename/ {print $4}' | tr -d '\r' | tr '\n' ' ' | xargs sudo grep -iH '^\s*clientaliveinterval'
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-stig.conf::ClientAliveInterval 600

Verify the runtime setting with the following command:

$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i clientaliveinterval
clientaliveinterval 600

If the "ClientAliveInterval" keyword is not set to a value of "600" or less in a drop-in that lexicographically precedes 50-redhat.conf, or if no output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to automatically terminate all network connections associated with SSH traffic at the end of a session or after 10 minutes of inactivity.

Note: This setting must be applied in conjunction with RHEL-10-700660 to function correctly.

In "/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d", create a drop file that will lexicographically precede 50-redhat.conf and add the following line:

ClientAliveInterval 600

Restart the SSH daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Terminating an idle SSH session within a short time period reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized personnel to take control of a management session enabled on the console or console port that has been left unattended. In addition, quickly terminating an idle SSH session will also free up resources committed by the managed network element.

Terminating network connections associated with communications sessions includes, for example, deallocating associated TCP/IP address/port pairs at the operating system level and deallocating networking assignments at the application level if multiple application sessions are using a single operating system-level network connection. This does not mean that the operating system terminates all sessions or network access; it only ends the inactive session and releases the resources associated with that session.

RHEL 10 uses "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" for configurations of OpenSSH. Within the "sshd_config", the product of the values of "ClientAliveInterval" and "ClientAliveCountMax" are used to establish the inactivity threshold.

The "ClientAliveInterval" is a timeout interval in seconds after which if no data has been received from the client, sshd will send a message through the encrypted channel to request a response from the client.

The "ClientAliveCountMax" is the number of client alive messages that may be sent without sshd receiving any messages back from the client. If this threshold is met, sshd will disconnect the client.

For more information on these settings and others, refer to the sshd_config man pages.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000163-GPOS-00072, SRG-OS-000279-GPOS-00109, SRG-OS-000395-GPOS-00175

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001133**: Terminate the network connection associated with a communications session at the end of the session or after an organization-defined time period of inactivity.  
  Rev 5: SC-10 · Rev 4: SC-10 · Rev 3: SC-10
- **CCI-002361**: Automatically terminate a user session after organization-defined conditions or trigger events requiring session disconnect.  
  Rev 5: AC-12 · Rev 4: AC-12 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002891**: Verify session and network connection termination after the completion of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.  
  Rev 5: MA-4 (7) · Rev 4: MA-4 (7) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281297 · RHEL-10-700940 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must not default to the graphical display manager unless approved.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281297r1166843_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not default to the graphical display manager unless approved.

**Why it matters:** This decides what the sign-in screen shows and which shortcuts are allowed. For example, it hides the list of usernames, doesn't show who signed in last, and turns off "sign in automatically". It's like a hotel front desk that won't tell a stranger which room a guest is in.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, GDM and GNOME settings are managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/{gdm,local}.d/ with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. Examples include disable-user-list, disable-restart-buttons, and 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm/custom.conf. If no GUI is required, remove the GNOME and X packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** Users will need to type their username in full and can't use convenience sign-in methods. Hiding restart buttons on the logon screen means console users need credentials to reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to boot to the command line with the following command:

$ systemctl get-default
multi-user.target

If the system default target is not set to "multi-user.target", and the information system security officer lacks a documented requirement for a graphical user interface, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to boot to the command line by setting the default target to "multi-user" with the following command:

$ sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unnecessary service packages must not be installed to decrease the attack surface of the system. Graphical display managers have a long history of security vulnerabilities and must not be used unless approved and documented.

**Threat & control context:** The logon surface can leak information (usernames, the last logged-on user, local administrator lists) that cuts an attacker's effort in half, and convenience features (automatic logon, picture passwords, convenience PINs, password reveal buttons) weaken authentication assurance. These settings reduce information disclosure (AC-14, IA-6 authenticator feedback) and keep interactive logon on approved authenticators.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-281298 · RHEL-10-700950 · CAT I: RHEL 10 must disable the systemd Ctrl-Alt-Delete burst key sequence.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281298r1273604_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable the systemd Ctrl-Alt-Delete burst key sequence.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/systemd/system.conf.d | CtrlAltDelBurstAction | none |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set the GRUB2 superuser password with 'grub2-setpassword' (stored hashed in /boot/grub2/user.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/user.cfg) and set a unique superuser name in /etc/grub.d/01_users. Rescue and emergency modes must require root authentication (sulogin in rescue.service and emergency.service). Mask Ctrl-Alt-Del with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none' in systemd's system.conf. Mask debug-shell. kdump is disabled unless it's needed.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to not reboot the system when Ctrl-Alt-Delete is pressed seven times within two seconds with the following command:

$ sudo grep -iR CtrlAltDelBurstAction /etc/systemd/system*
/etc/systemd/system.conf.d/55-CtrlAltDel-BurstAction.conf:CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none

If the "CtrlAltDelBurstAction" is not set to "none", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to disable the CtrlAltDelBurstAction by adding it to a drop file in a "/etc/systemd/system.conf.d/" configuration file:

If no drop file exists, create one with the following command:

$ sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system.conf.d && sudo vi /etc/systemd/system.conf.d/55-CtrlAltDel-BurstAction.conf

Edit the file to contain the setting by adding the following text:

[Manager]
CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none

Reload the daemon for this change to take effect.

$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A locally logged-on user who presses Ctrl-Alt-Delete when at the console can reboot the system. If accidentally pressed, as could happen in the case of a mixed operating system environment, this can create the risk of short-term loss of availability of systems due to unintentional reboot.

In a graphical user environment, risk of unintentional reboot from the Ctrl-Alt-Delete sequence is reduced because the user will be prompted before any action is taken.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, set the GRUB2 superuser password with 'grub2-setpassword' (stored hashed in /boot/grub2/user.cfg or /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/user.cfg) and set a unique superuser name in /etc/grub.d/01_users. Rescue and emergency modes must require root authentication (sulogin in rescue.service and emergency.service). Mask Ctrl-Alt-Del with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'CtrlAltDelBurstAction=none' in systemd's system.conf. Mask debug-shell. kdump is disabled unless it's needed.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that the current GRUB 2 configuration disables the ability of systemd to spawn an interactive boot process with the following command:

$ sudo grubby --info=ALL | grep args | grep 'systemd.confirm_spawn'

If any output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that the current GRUB 2 configuration disables the ability of systemd to spawn an interactive boot process with the following command:

$ sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --remove-args="systemd.confirm_spawn"
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Using interactive or recovery boot, the console user could disable auditing, firewalls, or other services, weakening system security.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-281301 · RHEL-10-700990 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must disable virtual system calls.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281301r1184700_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000134-GPOS-00068 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations |
| CCI | CCI-001084 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-3 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable virtual system calls.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel tunables are set in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf (applied with 'sysctl --system' and verified with 'sysctl <key>'). Remember that a later file or /etc/sysctl.conf can override an earlier drop-in, and the STIG check typically greps all locations for conflicts. Boot parameters (e.g. 'vsyscall=none', 'page_poison=1', 'pti=on', 'slub_debug=P', 'audit=1') are set with 'grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=...'. Core dumps are controlled through /etc/systemd/coredump.conf and 'ulimit -c'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that the current GRUB 2 configuration disables virtual system calls with the following command:

$ sudo grubby --info=ALL | grep args | grep -v 'vsyscall=none'

If any output is returned, this is a finding.

Check that virtual system calls are disabled by default to persist in kernel updates with the following command:

$ sudo grep vsyscall /etc/default/grub
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="vsyscall=none"

If "vsyscall" is not set to "none", is missing or commented out, and is not documented with the information system security officer as an operational requirement, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to disable virtual system calls with the following command:

$ sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="vsyscall=none"
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** System calls are special routines in the Linux kernel, which userspace applications ask to do privileged tasks. Invoking a system call is an expensive operation because the processor must interrupt the currently executing task and switch context to kernel mode and then back to userspace after the system call completes. Virtual system calls map into user space a page that contains some variables and the implementation of some system calls. This allows the system calls to be executed in userspace to alleviate the context-switching expense.

Virtual system calls provide an opportunity of attack for a user who has control of the return instruction pointer. Disabling virtual system calls help to prevent return-oriented programming attacks via buffer overflows and overruns.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001084**: Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions.  
  Rev 5: SC-3 · Rev 4: SC-3 · Rev 3: SC-3

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must clear memory when it is freed to prevent use-after-free attacks.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel tunables are set in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf (applied with 'sysctl --system' and verified with 'sysctl <key>'). Remember that a later file or /etc/sysctl.conf can override an earlier drop-in, and the STIG check typically greps all locations for conflicts. Boot parameters (e.g. 'vsyscall=none', 'page_poison=1', 'pti=on', 'slub_debug=P', 'audit=1') are set with 'grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=...'. Core dumps are controlled through /etc/systemd/coredump.conf and 'ulimit -c'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured so that the current GRUB2 configuration mitigates use-after-free vulnerabilities by employing memory poisoning.

Check that the current GRUB2 configuration mitigates use-after-free vulnerabilities by employing memory poisoning with the following command:

$ sudo grubby --info=ALL | grep args | grep -v init_on_free=1

If any output is returned, this is a finding.

Check that page poisoning is enabled by default to persist in kernel updates with the following command:

$ sudo grep grub_cmdline_linux /etc/default/grub
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="... init_on_free=1"

If "init_on_free=1" is missing or commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
$ sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="init_on_free=1"
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Some adversaries launch attacks with the intent of executing code in nonexecutable regions of memory or in memory locations that are prohibited. Security safeguards employed to protect memory include, for example, data execution prevention and address space layout randomization. Data execution prevention safeguards can be either hardware-enforced or software-enforced, with hardware providing the greater strength of mechanism.

Poisoning writes an arbitrary value to freed pages, so any modification or reference to that page after being freed or before being initialized will be detected and prevented. This prevents many types of use-after-free vulnerabilities at little performance cost. It also prevents data leakage and detection of corrupted memory.

"init_on_free" is a Linux kernel boot parameter that enhances security by initializing memory regions when they are freed, preventing data leakage. This process ensures that stale data in freed memory cannot be accessed by malicious programs.

SLUB canaries add a randomized value (canary) at the end of SLUB-allocated objects to detect memory corruption caused by buffer overflows or underflows. Redzoning adds padding (red zones) around SLUB-allocated objects to detect overflows or underflows by triggering a fault when adjacent memory is accessed. SLUB canaries are often more efficient and provide stronger detection against buffer overflows compared to redzoning. SLUB canaries are supported in hardened Linux kernels such as the ones provided by Linux-hardened.

SLAB objects are blocks of physically contiguous memory. SLUB is the unqueued SLAB allocator.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

The control of information in shared resources is also commonly referred to as object reuse and residual information protection.

This requirement generally applies to the design of an information technology product, but it can also apply to the configuration of information system components that are, or use, such products. This can be verified by acceptance/validation processes in DoW or other government agencies.

There may be shared resources with configurable protections (e.g., files in storage) that may be assessed on specific information system components.

```text
Check the status of the "kernel.perf_event_paranoid" kernel parameter:

$ sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid
kernel.perf_event_paranoid = 2

If "kernel.perf_event_paranoid" is not set to "2" or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to prevent kernel profiling by nonprivileged users.

Create a drop-in if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/99-kernel_perf_event_paranoid.conf

Add the following to the file:

kernel.perf_event_paranoid = 2

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Preventing unauthorized information transfers mitigates the risk of information, including encrypted representations of information, produced by the actions of prior users/roles (or the actions of processes acting on behalf of prior users/roles) from being available to any current users/roles (or current processes) that obtain access to shared system resources (e.g., registers, main memory, hard disks) after those resources have been released back to information systems. The control of information in shared resources is also commonly referred to as object reuse and residual information protection.

This requirement generally applies to the design of an information technology product, but it can also apply to the configuration of information system components that are, or use, such products. This can be verified by acceptance/validation processes in DoW or other government agencies.

There may be shared resources with configurable protections (e.g., files in storage) that may be assessed on specific information system components.

Setting the "kernel.perf_event_paranoid" kernel parameter to "2" prevents attackers from gaining additional system information as a nonprivileged user.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000132-GPOS-00067, SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001082**: Separate user functionality, including user interface services, from system management functionality.  
  Rev 5: SC-2 · Rev 4: SC-2 · Rev 3: SC-2
- **CCI-001090**: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.  
  Rev 5: SC-4 · Rev 4: SC-4 · Rev 3: SC-4

### V-281307 · RHEL-10-701050 · CAT I: RHEL 10 must prevent the loading of a new kernel for later execution.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281307r1268241_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000366-GPOS-00153 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations |
| CCI | CCI-003992 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-14 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent the loading of a new kernel for later execution.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.d/99-kernel_kexec_load_disabled.conf | kernel.kexec_load_disabled | 1 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel tunables are set in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf (applied with 'sysctl --system' and verified with 'sysctl <key>'). Remember that a later file or /etc/sysctl.conf can override an earlier drop-in, and the STIG check typically greps all locations for conflicts. Boot parameters (e.g. 'vsyscall=none', 'page_poison=1', 'pti=on', 'slub_debug=P', 'audit=1') are set with 'grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=...'. Core dumps are controlled through /etc/systemd/coredump.conf and 'ulimit -c'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is configured to disable kernel image loading.

Check the status of the "kernel.kexec_load_disabled" kernel parameter with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl kernel.kexec_load_disabled
kernel.kexec_load_disabled = 1

If "kernel.kexec_load_disabled" is not set to "1" or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to disable kernel image loading.

Create a drop-in if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/99-kernel_kexec_load_disabled.conf

Add the following to the file:

kernel.kexec_load_disabled = 1

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Changes to any software components can have significant effects on the overall security of the operating system. This requirement ensures the software has not been tampered with and has been provided by a trusted vendor.

Disabling kexec_load prevents an unsigned kernel image (that could be a windows kernel or modified vulnerable kernel) from being loaded. Kexec can be used to subvert the entire secureboot process and should be avoided at all costs, especially because it can load unsigned kernel images.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-003992**: Prevent the installation of organization-defined software and firmware components without verification that the component has been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.  
  Rev 5: CM-14 · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281312 · RHEL-10-701100 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured to disable the Controller Area Network (CAN) kernel module.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281312r1167086_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Unneeded Kernel Modules & Protocols |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to disable the Controller Area Network (CAN) kernel module.

**Why it matters:** The core of the operating system can load optional add-ons on demand, including some that are rarely used and not well tested. This rule simply removes the ability to load add-ons you'll never need, like boarding up doors in a building that nobody uses, so there are fewer ways in.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/modprobe.d/can.conf | blacklist | can |

**How it works:** Create /etc/modprobe.d/<name>.conf containing 'install <module> /bin/false' (prevents loading) and 'blacklist <module>' (prevents auto-loading by alias). Check with 'modprobe -n -v <module>' and 'lsmod | grep <module>'. Unload any currently loaded module with 'modprobe -r'.

**Operational impact:** Confirm that no workload needs the module (for example, SCTP is used by some telecom applications and CAN by vehicle and industrial interfaces) before blocking it.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 disables the ability to load the CAN kernel module with the following command:

$ sudo grep -rs can /etc/modprobe.conf /etc/modprobe.d/* | grep -v '#'
```

```text
blacklist sctp
```
