### V-281336 · RHEL-10-800040 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must securely compare internal information system clocks at least every 24 hours.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281336r1273614_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000355-GPOS-00143 |
| Topic | Time Synchronization |
| CCI | CCI-004923, CCI-004926, CCI-001890, CCI-004922 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-45 (1) (a), SC-45 (1) (b), AU-8 b, SC-45 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-8 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must securely compare internal information system clocks at least every 24 hours.

**Why it matters:** This keeps the computer's clock exactly in step with an official time source. That might sound minor, but security logs from different computers can only be pieced together if every clock agrees, and some sign-in systems refuse to work when clocks drift. It's like making sure all the witnesses' watches show the same time.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *NTP / chrony*: Network Time Protocol: how computers keep their clocks accurate over the network.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/chrony.conf | server | [ntp.server.name] iburst maxpoll 16 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, chronyd is configured in /etc/chrony.conf: use 'server <DoD-time-source> iburst maxpoll 16', 'port 0' (don't act as a server) and 'cmdport 0'. Verify with 'chronyc sources -v' and 'timedatectl'. Time stamps should map to UTC/GMT.

**Operational impact:** Large clock corrections can confuse running applications. chrony slews gradually by default. Make sure the time servers are reachable through the firewall (UDP 123).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is securely comparing internal information system clocks at least every 24 hours with an NTP server with the following commands:

$ sudo grep maxpoll /etc/chrony.conf
server 0.us.pool.ntp.mil iburst maxpoll 16

If the "maxpoll" option is set to a number greater than 16, or the line is missing or commented out, this is a finding.

Verify the "chrony.conf" file is configured to an authoritative DoW time source by running the following command:

$ sudo grep -i server /etc/chrony.conf
server 0.us.pool.ntp.mil

If the parameter "server" is not set or is not set to an authoritative DoW time source, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to securely compare internal information system clocks at least every 24 hours with an NTP server by adding/modifying the following line in the "/etc/chrony.conf" file:

server [ntp.server.name] iburst maxpoll 16
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inaccurate time stamps make it more difficult to correlate events and can lead to an inaccurate analysis. Determining the correct time a particular event occurred on a system is critical when conducting forensic analysis and investigating system events. Sources outside the configured acceptable allowance (drift) may be inaccurate.

Synchronizing internal information system clocks provides uniformity of time stamps for information systems with multiple system clocks and systems connected over a network.

Depending on the infrastructure being used, the "pool" directive may not be supported.

Authoritative time sources include the United States Naval Observatory (USNO) time servers, a time server designated for the appropriate DoW network (NIPRNet/SIPRNet), and/or the Global Positioning System (GPS).

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000355-GPOS-00143, SRG-OS-000356-GPOS-00144, SRG-OS-000359-GPOS-00146, SRG-OS-000785-GPOS-00250

**Threat & control context:** Accurate, synchronized time underpins log correlation across systems, Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validity checks and forensic timelines (AU-8, AU-8(1) synchronization with an authoritative source, AU-8(2) secondary source). Time sources should be authenticated where possible and restricted to client mode, so the host can't be abused as an NTP amplifier.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.006 Indicator Removal: Timestomp

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004923**: Compare the internal system clocks on an organization-defined frequency with organization-defined authoritative time source.  
  Rev 5: SC-45 (1) (a) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-004926**: Synchronize the internal system clocks to the authoritative time source when the time difference is greater than organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: SC-45 (1) (b) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001890**: Record time stamps for audit records that use Coordinated Universal Time, have a fixed local time offset from Coordinated Universal Time, or that include the local time offset as part of the time stamp.  
  Rev 5: AU-8 b · Rev 4: AU-8 b · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-004922**: Synchronize system clocks within and between systems or system components.  
  Rev 5: SC-45 · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281337 · RHEL-10-800050 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must enable hardening for the Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) just-in-time compiler.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281337r1167161_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000433-GPOS-00192 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations, Host Firewall |
| CCI | CCI-002824 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-16 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-16 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enable hardening for the Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) just-in-time compiler.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.d/99-net_core-bpf_jit_harden.conf | net.core.bpf_jit_harden | 2 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, kernel tunables are set in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf (applied with 'sysctl --system' and verified with 'sysctl <key>'). Remember that a later file or /etc/sysctl.conf can override an earlier drop-in, and the STIG check typically greps all locations for conflicts. Boot parameters (e.g. 'vsyscall=none', 'page_poison=1', 'pti=on', 'slub_debug=P', 'audit=1') are set with 'grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args=...'. Core dumps are controlled through /etc/systemd/coredump.conf and 'ulimit -c'.

**Also related (Host Firewall):** On RHEL, use firewalld (systemctl enable --now firewalld) with nftables as the backend (FirewallBackend=nftables in /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf). Set the default zone to drop or deny and add only the required services and ports ('firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=...', then '--reload'). Review with 'firewall-cmd --list-all-zones'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enables hardening for the BPF JIT compiler.

Check the status of the "net.core.bpf_jit_harden" parameter with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl net.core.bpf_jit_harden
net.core.bpf_jit_harden = 2

If "net.core.bpf_jit_harden" is not equal to "2" or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to enable hardening for the BPF JIT compiler.

Create the drop-in file if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/99-net_core-bpf_jit_harden.conf

Add the following line to the file:

net.core.bpf_jit_harden = 2

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When hardened, the extended BPF just-in-time (JIT) compiler will randomize any kernel addresses in the BPF programs and maps, and will not expose the JIT addresses in "/proc/kallsyms".

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution; T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002824**: Implement organization-defined controls to protect the system memory from unauthorized code execution.  
  Rev 5: SI-16 · Rev 4: SI-16 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-281338 · RHEL-10-800060 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must have at least two name servers configured for systems using Domain Name Server (DNS) resolution.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281338r1167164_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186 |
| Topic | Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-002385 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-5 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-5 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have at least two name servers configured for systems using Domain Name Server (DNS) resolution.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *IP*: Internet Protocol: the addressing system that routes data between computers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/resolv.conf | nameserver | [name server 1] |
| Config | /etc/resolv.conf | nameserver | [name server 2] |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If the system is running in a cloud platform and the cloud provider gives a single, highly available IP address for DNS configuration, this control is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 has at least two name servers configured for systems using DNS resolution.

Verify the name servers used by the system with the following command:

$ sudo grep nameserver /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 192.168.1.2
nameserver 192.168.1.3

If fewer than two lines are returned that are not commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use two or more name servers for DNS resolution based on the DNS mode of the system.

If the NetworkManager DNS mode is set to "none", add the following lines to "/etc/resolv.conf":

nameserver [name server 1]
nameserver [name server 2]

Replace [name server 1] and [name server 2] with the IPs of two different DNS resolvers.

If the NetworkManager DNS mode is set to "default", add two DNS servers to a NetworkManager connection using the following command:

$ nmcli connection modify [connection name] ipv4.dns [name server 1],[name server 2]

Replace [name server 1] and [name server 2] with the IPs of two different DNS resolvers.

Replace [connection name] with a valid NetworkManager connection name on the system.

Replace ipv4 with ipv6 if IPv6 DNS servers are used.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To provide availability for name resolution services, multiple redundant name servers are mandated. A failure in name resolution could lead to the failure of security functions requiring name resolution, which may include time synchronization, centralized authentication, and remote system logging.

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a

**How it works:** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Verify RHEL 10 does not have unauthorized IP tunnels configured.

### V-281342 · RHEL-10-800100 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must not forward Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) source-routed packets.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281342r1167176_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186 |
| Topic | Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-002385, CCI-001097 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-5 a, SC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-5, SC-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not forward Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) source-routed packets.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.
- *IP*: Internet Protocol: the addressing system that routes data between computers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv4_accept_source.conf | net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route | 0 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 will not accept IPv4 source-routed packets.

Check the value of the "net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route" variable with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0

If "net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route" is not set to "0" or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to ignore IPv4 source-routed packets.

Create a configuration file if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv4_accept_source.conf

Add the following line to the file:

net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Source-routed packets allow the source of the packet to suggest that routers forward the packet along a different path than configured on the router, which can be used to bypass network security measures. This requirement applies only to the forwarding of source-routed traffic, such as when IPv4 forwarding is enabled and the system is functioning as a router.

Accepting source-routed packets in the IPv4 protocol has few legitimate uses. It must be disabled unless it is absolutely required.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186, SRG-OS-000142-GPOS-00073

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001097**: Monitor and control communications at the external managed interfaces to the system and at key managed interfaces within the system.  
  Rev 5: SC-7 a · Rev 4: SC-7 a · Rev 3: SC-7 a

### V-281343 · RHEL-10-800110 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must log Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) packets with impossible addresses.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281343r1167179_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-002385, CCI-001098 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-5 a, SC-7 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-5, SC-7 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-7 b |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must log Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) packets with impossible addresses.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.
- *IP*: Internet Protocol: the addressing system that routes data between computers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv4_log_martians.conf | net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians | 1 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Also related (Network Stack Hardening):** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 logs IPv4 martian packets.

Check the value of the "net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians" variable with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians
net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1

If "net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians" is not set to "1" or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to log martian packets on IPv4 interfaces.

Create a configuration file if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv4_log_martians.conf

Add the following line to the file:

net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The presence of "martian" packets (which have impossible addresses), as well as spoofed packets, source-routed packets, and redirects, could be a sign of nefarious network activity. Logging these packets enables this activity to be detected.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186, SRG-OS-000142-GPOS-00074

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001098**: Connect to external networks or systems only through managed interfaces consisting of boundary protection devices arranged in accordance with an organizational security architecture.  
  Rev 5: SC-7 c · Rev 4: SC-7 c · Rev 3: SC-7 b

| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv4_accept_source_route.conf | net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route | 0 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 does not accept IPv4 source-routed packets by default.

Check the value of the "net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route" variable with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0

If "net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route" is not set to "0" or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to not forward IPv4 source-routed packets by default.

Create a configuration file if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv4_accept_source_route.conf

Add the following line to the file:

net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Source-routed packets allow the source of the packet to suggest routers forward the packet along a different path than configured on the router, which can be used to bypass network security measures.

Accepting source-routed packets in the IPv4 protocol has few legitimate uses. It must be disabled unless it is absolutely required, such as when IPv4 forwarding is enabled and the system is legitimately functioning as a router.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186, SRG-OS-000142-GPOS-00078

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001102**: Implement a managed interface for each external telecommunication service.  
  Rev 5: SC-7 (4) (a) · Rev 4: SC-7 (4) (a) · Rev 3: SC-7 (4) (a)

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must use a reverse-path filter for Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) network traffic when possible by default.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.
- *IP*: Internet Protocol: the addressing system that routes data between computers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|

**How it works:** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 uses reverse path filtering on IPv4 interfaces.

Check the value of the "net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter" with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

If the returned line does not have a value of "1", or a line is not returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use reverse path filtering on IPv4 interfaces by default.

Create a configuration file if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/ipv4_rp_filter.conf

Add the following line to the file:

net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enabling reverse path filtering drops packets with source addresses that should not have been able to be received on the interface on which they were received. It must not be used on systems that are routers for complicated networks but is helpful for end hosts and routers serving small networks.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186, SRG-OS-000142-GPOS-00079

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-281353 · RHEL-10-800210 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must not enable Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) packet forwarding unless the system is a router.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281353r1167209_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186 |
| Topic | Network Stack Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-002385, CCI-001108 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-5 a, SC-7 (4) (e) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-5, SC-7 (4) (e) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-7 (4) (f) |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not enable Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) packet forwarding unless the system is a router.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.
- *IP*: Internet Protocol: the addressing system that routes data between computers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.d/ipv4_forwarding.conf | net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding | 0 |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 is not performing IPv4 packet forwarding unless the system is a router.

Check that "net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding" is disabled using the following command:

$ sudo sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding
net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding = 0

If "net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding" is not set to "0" and is not documented with the information system security officer as an operational requirement or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to not allow IPv4 packet forwarding unless the system is a router.

Create a configuration file if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/ipv4_forwarding.conf

Add the following line to the file:

net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding = 0

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Routing protocol daemons are typically used on routers to exchange network topology information with other routers. If this capability is used when not required, system network information may be transmitted unnecessarily across the network.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186, SRG-OS-000142-GPOS-00084

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002385**: Protect against or limit the effects of organization-defined types of denial-of-service events.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 a · Rev 4: SC-5 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001108**: Remove traffic flow policy exceptions that are no longer supported by an explicit mission or business need for each external telecommunication service.  
  Rev 5: SC-7 (4) (e) · Rev 4: SC-7 (4) (e) · Rev 3: SC-7 (4) (f)

$ sudo sysctl net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra = 0

If "net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra" is not set to "0" or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to not accept router advertisements on all IPv6 interfaces by default, unless the system is a router.

Create a configuration file if it does not already exist:

$ sudo vi /etc/sysctl.d/ipv6_accept_ra.conf

Add the following line to the file:

net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra = 0

Reload settings from all system configuration files with the following command:

$ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must protect against or limit the effects of denial-of-service (DoS) attacks by ensuring that rate-limiting measures on impacted network interfaces are implemented.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**Key terms:**
- *Firewall*: A filter that decides which network connections are allowed in or out.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf | FirewallBackend | nftables |

Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

Verify RHEL 10 protects against or limits the effects of DoS attacks by ensuring rate-limiting measures on impacted network interfaces are implemented.

FirewallBackend=nftables

If "nftables" is not set to "FirewallBackend", this is a finding.

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 so that "nftables" is the default "firewallbackend" for "firewalld" by adding or editing the following line in "/etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf":

FirewallBackend=nftables

Establish rate-limiting rules based on organization-defined types of DoS attacks on impacted network interfaces.

A variety of technologies exist to limit or, in some cases, eliminate the effects of DoS attacks (e.g., limiting processes or establishing memory partitions). Employing increased capacity and bandwidth, combined with service redundancy, may reduce the susceptibility to some DoS attacks.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/NetworkManager/NetworkManager.conf | dns | none |

**How it works:** On RHEL, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 has a DNS mode configured in Network Manager.

$ NetworkManager --print-config
[main]
dns=none

If the dns key under "main" does not exist or is set to "dnsmasq", this is a finding.

Note: If RHEL 10 is configured to use a DNS resolver other than Network Manager, the configuration must be documented and approved by the information system security officer.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to use a DNS mode in Network Manager.

In "/etc/NetworkManager/NetworkManager.conf", add the following line in the "[main]" section:

dns = none

Where <dns processing mode> is default, none, or systemd-resolved.

Network Manager must be reloaded for the change to take effect:

$ sudo systemctl reload NetworkManager
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To ensure that DNS resolver settings are respected, a DNS mode in Network Manager must be configured. The following are common DNS values in "NetworkManager.conf [main]":

- default: NetworkManager will update "/etc/resolv.conf" to reflect the nameservers provided by currently active connections.
- none: NetworkManager will not modify "/etc/resolv.conf". Used when DNS is managed manually or by another service.
- systemd-resolved: Uses "systemd-resolved" to manage DNS.
- dnsmasq: Enables the internal "dnsmasq" plugin.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000420-GPOS-00186, SRG-OS-000142-GPOS-00091

### V-281363 · RHEL-10-800310 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must be configured to operate in secure mode if the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server service is required.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281363r1195454_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000074-GPOS-00042 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software, System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000197 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to operate in secure mode if the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server service is required.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**How it works:** On RHEL, remove packages with 'dnf remove <pkg>' and verify with 'rpm -q <pkg>' (expect 'package <pkg> is not installed'). Watch for dependency cascades in the dnf transaction summary before confirming.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On RHEL, use 'systemctl enable --now <unit>' for required services and 'systemctl disable --now <unit>' plus 'systemctl mask <unit>' for prohibited ones. Masking prevents a service from being started manually or as a dependency. Check with 'systemctl is-enabled <unit>' and 'systemctl is-active <unit>', and remember the matching .socket units.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Note: If a TFTP server is not installed, this rule is not applicable.

Verify RHEL 10 is configured to operate in secure mode if the TFTP server service is required.

Determine if the TFTP server is installed with the following command:

$ sudo dnf list installed | grep tftp-server
tftp-server.x86_64                                   5.2-48.el10                     @rhel-10-for-x86_64-appstream-rpms

Verify that the TFTP daemon, if "tftp.server" is installed, is configured to operate in secure mode with the following command:

$ systemctl cat tftp.service | grep -i execstart
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/in.tftpd -s /var/lib/tftpboot

Note: The "-s" option ensures that the TFTP server serves only files from the specified directory, which is a security measure to prevent unauthorized access to other parts of the file system.

If the TFTP server is installed, but the TFTP daemon is not configured to operate in secure mode, and tftp is not documented as critical to the mission with the information system security officer, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 TFTP to operate in secure mode with the following command:

$ sudo systemctl edit tftp.service

In the editor, enter the following:

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/in.tftpd -s /var/lib/tftpboot

After making changes, reload the systemd daemon and restart the TFTP service as follows:

$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload
$ sudo systemctl restart tftp.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Restricting TFTP to a specific directory prevents remote users from copying, transferring, or overwriting system files.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter; T1543 Create or Modify System Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000197**: For password-based authentication, transmit passwords only over cryptographically-protected channels.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (c) · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (c) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (c)

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce mode "0640" or less for the "/etc/audit/auditd.conf" file to prevent unauthorized access.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | 0640 /etc/audit/auditd.conf |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On RHEL, use 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' to check mode and ownership, and 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp' to fix them. Find problems with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup' and 'find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000'. Default permissions for new files come from umask (077 in /etc/login.defs and the shell profiles). 'rpm --setperms <pkg>' restores packaged defaults.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify RHEL 10 enforces the mode of "/etc/audit/auditd.conf" with the following command:

$ sudo stat -c "%a %n" /etc/audit/auditd.conf
640 /etc/audit/auditd.conf

If "/etc/audit/auditd.conf" does not have a mode of "0640", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to set the mode of the "/etc/audit/auditd.conf" file to "0640" with the following command:

$ sudo chmod 0640 /etc/audit/auditd.conf
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the capability to restrict the roles and individuals that can select which events are audited, unauthorized personnel may be able to prevent the auditing of critical events. Misconfigured audits may degrade the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfigured audits may also make it more difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate the events relating to an incident or identify those responsible for one.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000171**: Allow organization-defined personnel or roles to select the event types that are to be logged by specific components of the system.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 b · Rev 4: AU-12 b · Rev 3: AU-12 b

### V-281365 · RHEL-10-900100 · CAT II: RHEL 10 must prevent unauthorized changes to the audit system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-281365r1167245_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000057-GPOS-00027 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, Software & File Integrity Verification |
| CCI | CCI-000162, CCI-000163, CCI-000164 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-9 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-9 |
| Implemented via | Audit rule |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent unauthorized changes to the audit system.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audit rule | /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules | -e 2 |  |

**How it works:** On RHEL, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Also related (Software & File Integrity Verification):** On RHEL, repositories must have 'gpgcheck=1' (/etc/dnf/dnf.conf and /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo) and 'localpkg_gpgcheck=1', with Red Hat GPG keys imported ('rpm -q gpg-pubkey'). AIDE is configured in /etc/aide.conf (rules should include acl, xattrs and sha512). Initialize with 'aide --init' and move the new database into place. Schedule 'aide --check' daily (cron or systemd timer) with notification to the SA/ISSO.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the RHEL 10 audit system prevents unauthorized changes with the following command:

$ sudo grep "^\s*[^#]" /etc/audit/audit.rules | tail -1
-e 2

If the audit system is not set to be immutable by adding the "-e 2" option to the end of "/etc/audit/audit.rules", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure RHEL 10 to protect the audit system from unauthorized changes.

Set the audit rules to be immutable by adding the following line to end of "/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules":

-e 2

Restart the audit daemon with the following command for the changes to take effect:

$ sudo service auditd restart
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unauthorized disclosure of audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, thus compromising its confidentiality.

Audit information includes all information (e.g., audit records, audit settings, audit reports) needed to successfully audit RHEL 10 system activity.

In immutable mode, unauthorized users cannot execute changes to the audit system to potentially hide malicious activity and then put the audit rules back. A system reboot would be noticeable, and a system administrator could then investigate the unauthorized changes.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000057-GPOS-00027, SRG-OS-000058-GPOS-00028, SRG-OS-000059-GPOS-00029

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary; T1014 Rootkit

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000162**: Protect audit information from unauthorized access.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-000163**: Protect audit information from unauthorized modification.
